items.title: Tracing Knowledge Lineage for Federated Unlearning under Mutual Distillation
items.abstract: An edge server and nearby devices can train language models of different sizes together by mutual distillation. Federated unlearning (FU) and unlearning for large language models (LLMs) execute a removal request on one model. Under mutual distillation, however, the effect of the removed data has been copied into many students, and their uploads teach it back to the corrected teacher. We propose Holder-level Erasure via Replication-weighted Delta-closure (HERD), which decides which holders must be corrected. HERD records a knowledge lineage graph from the transfers that the server already performs and weights each edge by its transfer type. It computes how many times the residual at each holder will be copied and selects the cheapest set of holders whose correction bounds the cumulative residual after the request. A transfer guard and a rejoin rule cover the holders left uncorrected or offline. We prove that partial correction suffices only when the copy number of the lineage graph is below one, that averaging alone never reaches one, and that the correction set remains valid under link outages. On TOFU, HERD leaves 18% to 52% less cumulative residual than the strongest baseline at 6% to 12% of its correction cost.

items.title: Translating HR practices to inclusion climate: the moderating role of inclusive leadership
items.abstract: Purpose Grounded in the Social Information Processing Theory (SIPT), the current study aims to examine the role of Diversity-focused HR Practices in promoting Inclusion Climate; simultaneously, it also investigates the role of Inclusive Leadership as a moderator in relationship explaining how it shapes inclusion at work. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional quantitative approach has been taken, and the survey data were collected from 232 professionals employed in Indian IT sector organizations. To perform the data analysis PLS-SEM was employed using SmartPLS4.1.0 software. Findings The findings reveal while diversity-focused HR practices contribute to fostering an inclusive climate, their impact depends significantly on leadership behavior. Inclusive leaders play a critical role in strengthening the effectiveness of these practices by shaping how employees experience inclusion in their teams. Practical implications The findings of the study imply the gravity that a leader holds in the workgroup. As exhibited by findings, leaders with their inclusive behavior act as a catalyst which transforms HR practices into an inclusive workplace. Therefore, investments in diversity policies must be accompanied by leadership development programs to convert formal initiatives into employees-lived workplace experience. Originality/value The study integrates HR practices and leadership perspectives by identifying inclusive leadership as a contextual boundary condition explaining variability in inclusion climate formation. This shifts scholarly attention from formal HR systems to the role of leaders as enablers of inclusion, demonstrating that leadership is a key mechanism through which diversity initiatives translate into meaningful workplace experiences, thereby providing a novel insight to the present literature.

items.title: Traveling with Darwin in the Age of AI: Handwritten Historical Imagination and Evolution Learning in Introductory Biology
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has complicated writing assignments in college science courses by making it easier for students to produce polished explanations without necessarily engaging deeply with course concepts. Rather than focusing only on preventing or detecting AI use, instructors need assignments that preserve the work of student thinking when AI is readily available. This article describes “A Letter from the HMS Beagle,” a low-stakes assignment used in a large introductory Biology II course. Students imagined themselves as traveling companions of Charles Darwin and wrote a one-page, handwritten letter explaining natural selection through scientific evidence and a historically framed narrative. AI use was permitted during preparation, but the final response had to be handwritten on a provided sheet and submitted in person. The assignment combined scientific explanation, evidence use, historical imagination, and a deliberate procedural constraint. Rather than attempting to make student writing AI-proof, the design emphasized explanation, interpretation, and personal engagement. The activity offers a practical model for preserving scientific thinking and student engagement in AI-mediated science classrooms.

items.title: Trust and adoption maturity: An analysis of industry perceptions on the generative AI competency gap among business graduates
items.abstract: This study maps the importance, perceived needs, and competency gap of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across four domains—Technical, Strategic, Ethical, Adaptive—and examines their associations with trust, adoption maturity, and industry context. Data were collected from 389 industry professionals in Indonesia using purposive and snowball sampling. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests. The results indicate relatively high perceived GenAI competency needs across all domains, with the largest perceived gaps in the Technical and Strategic domains. Trust in GenAI was positively associated with perceived competency needs across all four domains and with perceived competency gaps in the Technical, Strategic, and Adaptive domains, but not the Ethical domain. Adoption maturity was associated with differences in several dimensions of industry perceptions, particularly industry-perceived graduate readiness to adopt GenAI and perceived needs in the Adaptive and Strategic domains. Sectoral differences were limited, with significant variation observed only in industry-perceived graduate readiness. The study contributes an integrated perspective linking trust and adoption maturity with perceived GenAI competency needs and gaps in Indonesia, highlighting curricular areas that warrant greater attention to applied Technical and Strategic capabilities across organizational GenAI adoption stages.

items.title: Trust in AI-based Educational Technologies as a Predictor of Generative AI Acceptance in Science Teacher Education: A Cross-Sectional Survey Study
items.abstract: As the integration of artificial intelligence (AI)–based educational technologies into teaching and learning processes accelerates, trust has emerged as a key determinant of whether preservice teachers are willing to adopt these technologies. The present study aimed to examine the relationship between the perceived trust of pre-service science teachers in AI-based educational technologies and generative AI acceptance and to determine the predictive power of trust on acceptance. Grounded in the TAM, the study employed a cross-sectional correlational survey design to investigate the role of trust in acceptance processes. Data were collected from 270 pre-service science teachers enrolled in a science teacher education program at a university via an online questionnaire. The Trust in AI-Based Educational Technologies Scale (TAI-EdTech Trust) and the Generative AI Acceptance Scale (GAIA) were used for data collection. The findings revealed a moderate, positive, and statistically significant relationship between trust in AI-based educational technologies and GA acceptance, indicating that trust significantly predicted GA acceptance. The results highlight the importance of developing content in science teacher education programs that supports the safe, ethical, and pedagogically responsible use of generative AI tools.

items.title: TSRL: Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Continual Agent Training
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents excel at complex, multi-step tasks but suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual learning--acquiring new skills often degrades previously mastered capabilities. Existing post-training paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is sample-efficient but prone to severe forgetting, while Reinforcement Learning (RL) preserves prior capabilities but converges slowly without expert guidance. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trigger-based Supervised Reinforcement Learning (TSRL), a framework that integrates the strengths of both paradigms through an adaptive, state-dependent expert supervision mechanism. TSRL employs RL as the optimization backbone, activating SFT selectively on "hard states" where the policy fails. Theoretically, we show that restricting supervision to failure states derives an upper bound on the cumulative parameter updates, thereby reducing forgetting compared to full SFT. Empirically, TSRL achieves consistent gains across three agent benchmarks (ALFWorld, WebShop, and Deep Search) at both 7B and 32B scales. In continual learning scenarios, our method retains up to 9.6 points more capability on prior tasks than SFT->RL baselines, while matching or exceeding target-task performance.

items.title: Two Clocks, One Body: A Systematic Review of Sleep, Circadian Rhythms and Molecular Ageing
items.abstract: Purpose Sleep disturbance is increasingly proposed as a modifiable contributor to biological ageing, and device-measured sleep as a scalable marker of ageing risk. This project is a systematic review of human studies relating sleep and circadian characteristics to molecular markers of biological ageing. These markers are telomere length, DNA methylation (candidate-gene, global and epigenome-wide) and DNA-methylation-derived epigenetic clocks such as Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge and DunedinPACE. Questions 1. In humans of any age, are sleep and circadian characteristics associated with telomere length, DNA methylation or epigenetic age acceleration? 2. Do findings differ by sleep domain (duration, quality and insomnia, continuity, timing and circadian rhythm, sleep-disordered breathing), by measurement method (device-based, experimental, self-reported, genetic) and by life stage? 3. How certain is the evidence for each sleep domain and outcome? Methods - Search: a reproducible PubMed search (run 2 October 2026), supplemented by earlier searches of PubMed Central, the Cochrane Library and DOAJ. - Screening and extraction: two independent reviewers screened records against pre-specified eligibility criteria, and data were extracted and independently verified. - Synthesis and certainty: results are synthesised narratively by direction of effect (SWiM), with study appraisal informed by ROBINS-E and certainty rated with GRADE. - Reporting: the review follows PRISMA 2020. Status and transparency This is a retrospective registration. Searching, screening and data extraction were completed before registration. An earlier protocol draft limited exposures to smartphone- and wearable-derived sleep measures. The final scope includes all sleep-measurement methods, with device-based measurement analysed as a pre-specified subgroup. Large-language-model tools assisted with screening and extraction, and the human authors verify all decisions. Expected outcomes - A peer-reviewed systematic review identifying which sleep characteristics are most consistently linked to molecular ageing, and how certain that evidence is. - An evidence map of research gaps, particularly for consumer-wearable and smartphone-derived sleep data. - Open materials: the search strategy, screening decisions, extraction tables and eligibility rules. Authors: Aruna Dey (ORCID 0009-0005-4679-084X), Rohan Rajiv (ORCID 0000-0001-7533-381X)

items.title: Uncertainty-Driven Selective Prediction with Auditable Human Deferral for EEG Decoding of Participant-Rated Occupational Risk
items.abstract: Large-language-model (LLM) layers are increasingly appended to electroencephalography (EEG) decoders, although their decision contribution is often unclear. We evaluate an uncertainty-driven architecture in which a calibrated EEG classifier predicts participants’ own four-level occupational-risk keypress ratings, a deterministic rule either retains or defers a prediction, and a template or optional LLM renders an auditable report. The objective is not to replace a previously published classifier benchmark on the shared EEG archive, but to evaluate downstream decisions from a fixed frozen-representation decoder. The analysis used 2634 response-inclusive 3 s epochs from 31 retained workers. Subject-grouped three-fold evaluation yielded balanced accuracy of 0.6336 (95% CI 0.5745–0.6622) and accuracy of 0.6875. Peak probability distinguished correct from incorrect predictions only moderately (AUC 0.6529), and the coverage-risk relationship was non-monotonic. At tau = 0.5, 71.49% of trials were retained (balanced accuracy of 0.6829); with illustrative under-estimation/over-estimation/deferral costs of 5/0.5/1, normalized cost fell from 0.5816 to 0.5363, but sensitivity analysis showed that benefit depends on the cost setting and threshold. A rule engine reproduced all evaluated LLM risk/deferral decisions, while a deterministic template matched the prespecified reporting checks; therefore, no decision-performance advantage of the LLM was demonstrated. The study supports cross-participant prediction within the shared experimental setting, not stimulus-disjoint generalization or objective workplace-risk prediction. Because response timestamps and actual supervisor decisions were unavailable, motor/visual confounding cannot be excluded and the human handoff remains a simulated policy rather than a human–AI team evaluation.

items.title: Understanding Early Attitudes Towards Generative AI Regulation in Higher Education: The Role of Academic Scientists’ Experience and Risk Perceptions
items.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology rapidly permeates higher education, it creates opportunities to transform teaching, research, and workforce preparation while raising ethical, social and environmental concerns. Academic scientists have a unique role in this transition as their early exposure to publicly accessible GenAI tools shapes emerging practices, norms, and institutional responses. Existing research often treats AI‐related risk as a single construct, limiting understanding of how distinct risk dimensions shape regulatory preferences. This study investigates how academic scientists’ experience with GenAI relates to risk perceptions over agency loss and data breach, and how these perceptions are associated with their regulatory attitudes during its formative stage. Using survey data collected between September and November 2023, shortly after ChatGPT became widely accessible, we find that greater GenAI experience is associated with lower perceived risks. Meanwhile, different risk perceptions are linked to distinct regulatory preferences: perceived risk of agency loss is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation and a lower likelihood of supporting academic self‐regulation, whereas perceived data breach risk is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation but not associated with the likelihood of supporting self‐regulation. These findings provide an early baseline understanding of faculty attitudes toward GenAI regulation in academic contexts.

items.title: Understanding how and where AI can enhance the effectiveness of PMM-mediated organisational change: a conceptual framework
items.abstract: Purpose To develop a social complexity-based understanding of how and where artificial intelligence (AI) and generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can enhance the effectiveness of performance measurement and management (PMM) mediated organisational change. Design/methodology/approach This article draws on a social complexity interpretation of PMM, conviction narrative theory and the AI and GAI literature, to present a conceptualisation of AI-augmented PMM-mediated organisational change that describes how and where machine-based and human-based decision-making processes can augment performance measurement systems and performance management practices. Findings AI's and GAI's inability to replicate human reflexivity and judgement in equivocal and indeterminate situations limits what these technologies can do in PMM-mediated organisational change. AI and GAI can augment decision-making processes associated with performance measurement and the execution of performance management-initiated interventions; however, creating these interventions relies on human reflexivity and judgement. Originality/value This conceptual investigation highlights the limitations of AI and GAI technologies in PMM-mediated organisational change and explains why human-based decision-making continues to play a distinctive role. It contributes to our understanding of how AI and GAI can influence organisational change in general, and performance management in particular, with implications for PMM researchers and practitioners.

items.title: Understanding Human-AI Trust in Military AI Applications: A Multistage Human Factors Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in military systems to support intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, autonomous operations, logistics, command and control, and decision support. Effective use, however, depends not only on technical performance but also on how operators perceive, interpret, evaluate, and rely on AI outputs under uncertainty, time pressure, and adversarial interference. This study presents a conceptual integrative review informed by a structured supplementary literature search and synthesis. It synthesizes human factors, human–automation trust, human–AI teaming, military AI, and industrial engineering literature to develop an iterative multistage framework of human–AI trust in military applications. Trust is conceptualized as dynamic situational trust in a specific military AI system during task interaction, while dispositional, initial, and learned trust are treated as antecedent conditions. The framework distinguishes four analytically separable but functionally interdependent stages—perception, interpretation, evaluation, and trust judgment and reliance decision—and identifies four military-relevant moderators: system transparency, explainability, and behavioral predictability; data quality and information uncertainty; adversarial vulnerability; and operational and organizational context. The framework clarifies conceptual pathways to calibrated reliance, overtrust, and undertrust, and derives implications for task analysis, interface evaluation, human-centered design, operator training, and empirical validation.

items.title: Understanding tourist satisfaction in craft-based cultural tourism: a hybrid PLS-SEM, ANN and explainable AI approach
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze the linear structural relationships and nonlinear predictive contributions associated with tourist satisfaction in the Trusmi Batik Tourism Area. By integrating PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI, it evaluates how destination attributes function as hygiene or motivator factors. The ultimate goal is to develop a strategic quadrant matrix to guide local governments and destination managers in optimizing craft-based cultural tourism management. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a multi-stage hybrid design integrating PLS-SEM, an MLP-based artificial neural network (ANN) and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) using SHAP analysis. PLS-SEM evaluates linear structural relationships based on the proposed theoretical hypotheses. A parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN captures complex, nonlinear predictive patterns. Finally, SHAP values interpret the model's hidden predictive contributions to construct an actionable strategic quadrant matrix. Findings The findings suggest that accessibility, resources, and the environment emerged as the primary “Star” motivators, with accessibility showing the strongest structural contribution and predictive importance among the examined constructs (ß = 0.310; |ϕ| = 0.416). “Batik Arts” emerged as the most influential indicator within the dataset. Services occupied the “Foundation” quadrant, whereas Facilities functioned primarily as a baseline hygiene factor and did not exhibit a statistically significant structural relationship with tourist satisfaction (ß = 0.014, p = 0.888). The parsimonious single-hidden-layer ANN demonstrated promising predictive performance in capturing nonlinear patterns within this exploratory dataset. Research limitations/implications This study integrates PLS-SEM, ANN, and SHAP-based XAI to examine linear and nonlinear patterns associated with tourist satisfaction within craft-based cultural tourism destinations. The findings suggest prioritizing immersive batik workshops, walkable heritage corridors, digital visitor information, and routine maintenance of basic facilities. The small, geographically focused sample limits generalizability and supports the need for external validation using larger and more diverse datasets. Practical implications This study offers a practical reference for tourism operators and local authorities to improve strategic resource allocation. Instead of funding costly luxury hotel expansions, managers could prioritize maintaining hygiene assets, including toilets, seating, and worship facilities. To enhance visitor satisfaction, investments may emphasize “Star” motivators through immersive batik-making workshops and authentic cultural experiences. Local governments may also improve urban micro-mobility by developing walkable sidewalks and flexible motorcycle routes throughout Trusmi's historic heritage corridors. These evidence-based recommendations support sustainable destination management while strengthening visitor experiences, cultural preservation, and long-term tourism resilience. Social implications This study has social implications for sustaining craft-based cultural tourism while strengthening community participation and cultural identity. The findings highlight the importance of accessible public spaces, immersive batik-making experiences, reliable visitor services, and heritage storytelling in supporting visitor engagement. Prioritizing these attributes can help local governments and tourism operators create more inclusive tourism environments that benefit visitors, artisans, and local communities. The framework also supports balanced resource allocation between basic hygiene facilities and culturally distinctive motivators. By strengthening artisan involvement, digital cultural communication, and heritage preservation, the approach can contribute to community resilience, intergenerational knowledge transmission, and sustainable tourism development. Originality/value The value of this study lies in its innovative hybrid framework integrating PLS-SEM, MLP-based ANN, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) within cultural tourism research. Compared with conventional linear approaches, the framework combines structural relationships, nonlinear predictive patterns, and SHAP-based interpretability to identify destination attributes with different levels of strategic importance.

items.title: Unethical Issues in the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Among Undergraduates in Public Universities of Cross River State, Nigeria
items.abstract: The objective of the study is to investigate unethical issues in the use of Artificial intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public Universities in Cross River State. The study was conducted in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. Survey research design was adopted of the study. The population of this study comprised all final year students in the two public Universities in Cross River State. The population of final year students in University of Calabar and University of Cross River State comprised of 7,020 undergraduate students as recorded by Academic Planning Unit & Management Information System, 2023/2024 of the respective Universities. Stratified random sampling was adopted for the study. A total sample of 409 students which constitute 10% of the population of students in the study area sampling from population of 4081 students from fifty three (53) departments of University of Calabar and University of Cross River State. A questionnaire titled Unethical issues in the Use of Artificial intelligence Questionnaire (UIUAIQ) was developed by the researchers. This was subjected to face and content validity by three experts in measurement and evaluation in Faculty of Education University of Calabar. A trial tested on fifty (50) students from College of Health Technology Calabar to establish the reliability of the instrument. Cronbach Alpha coefficient was used to determine the reliability estimate of the instrument α = .70-.72. The instrument was administered to the respondents and retrieved with Zero attrition rate. This process was facilitated by the researcher and two trained research assistants. The data collected was analyzed through descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation. The findings of this study reveal a significant prevalence of unethical issues in the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) among undergraduates in public universities in Cross River State. Furthermore, the study also indicates a high level of overreliance on AI technologies among undergraduates, leading to reduced engagement in academic tasks and a decline in deep learning experiences. Based on the findings, it was recommended among others that Higher institutions should incorporate AI ethics education into their curriculum to sensitize students about the ethical implications of AI misuse.

items.title: Using AI, Doubting AI: Developer Mental Models and Trust in AI-Assisted Software Work
items.abstract: Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.

items.title: Using Generative Artificial Intelligence to Craft Patient-Facing Report Summaries: Opportunities for Enhancing Resident Training
items.abstract: IntroductionEffective patient communication is an essential skill for radiology and nuclear medicine specialists, yet it remains underemphasized in residency training. With increasing patient access to electronic medical records, the ability to translate technical reports into patient-facing summaries is critical. Generative AI may offer a dual benefit of improving workflow by producing patient-appropriate summaries and serving as a training tool to help residents hone their communication skills. MethodsSeventy-six de-identified nuclear medicine imaging procedure reports (covering general nuclear medicine, PET/CT (positron emission tomography-computed tomography), and nuclear cardiology) were used to generate 608 patient-facing summaries: four versions of each report were generated using ChatGPT models (o1-mini, 4o, 4o-mini, 4 legacy) and four versions were written by residents. Summaries adhered to a four-sentence maximum and targeted a sixth-grade reading level. GPT-4o was used to critique and rank AI-generated summaries, and the two best-performing AI versions were compared with resident summaries. Blinded evaluations by three experienced nuclear medicine physicians assessed summaries on readability, accuracy, appropriateness, and overall fitness for purpose. Likelihood Ratio Chi-Square tests assessed differences in performance. ResultsGPT o1-mini was ranked as the best summary in 86% of initial AI comparisons and 100% of final comparative assessments with resident summaries. GPT 4o and o1-mini outperformed residents across multiple domains including clarity, health literacy, and tone. The best human summaries were consistently outperformed by AI in both physician and AI assessments, though discrepancies in ranking priorities (e.g., tolerance for jargon vs. inaccuracy) were noted and AI more often produced summaries containing misinterpretations of data in the original reports. Resident summaries showed wide variation in tone, technicality, and patient appropriateness. Overall, 65% of all summaries (AI and human) were deemed fit-for-purpose. ConclusionGenerative AI models can produce consistently appropriate and readable patient-facing summaries of imaging procedure reports and may serve as effective tools to develop resident communication skills. Generative AI may therefore model best practices and provide timely feedback, offering structured opportunities to refine written communication. Future work should explore its integration into learner-tailored educational constructs using frameworks such as Bloom’s taxonomy, to enhance resident training and effectiveness of feedback mechanisms.

items.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education: Insights from ASLP students
items.abstract: Background Emerging artificial intelligence-based technologies are increasingly influencing teaching and learning practices in healthcare education, offering new opportunities for student engagement, learning, and skill development. Objective The purpose of this study was to explore utilization of artificial intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education based on insights from students. Further, to explore their awareness, use, perceived benefits, barriers, and attitudes toward the integration of artificial intelligence. Method A cross-sectional online survey of 17 questions was distributed to 483 audiology and speech-language pathology students enrolled in undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes across multiple institutions in India through social media platforms. The questionnaire was developed following a review of previously published studies examining students’ perceptions of the implications of artificial intelligence in education. Descriptive analysis was used to analyse the findings. Results A total of 286 students participated in the study (mean age = 21.73 ± 2.33 years), of whom 82.2% were females. Most participants (96.9%) were aware of artificial intelligence technologies, and 89.9% indicated using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. Regarding the future role of artificial intelligence in education, 75.1% disagreed that it could replace human lecturers. Students primarily used it for assignments and exam preparation, while limited institutional acceptance was a major barrier to its implementation. Conclusions Students expressed an optimistic view regarding the application of artificial intelligence in education. Students reported concerns about inaccurate artificial intelligence-generated information, while limited acceptance, inadequate knowledge, and ethical concerns hindered its effective integration into education.

items.title: Value creation and capture in artificial intelligence‐enabled ecosystems
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We develop an ecosystem perspective on AI‐enabled value creation, grounded in AI's characteristics as a general‐purpose technology. We consider that AI can support multiple value propositions realized through distinct but interconnected ecosystems. Within this structure, AI innovators face choices concerning which value propositions to support, whether to pursue them through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make those offers open or closed. Users, in turn, are strategic actors facing choices among alternative ecosystem configurations of focal offers and complements through which the same value proposition might be realized. These choices by innovators and users may alter ecosystem roles and competitive relationships over time. We conclude by outlining research opportunities for strategy and innovation scholars examining how firms create and capture value in AI‐enabled ecosystems. Managerial Summary Value creation with AI depends not only on the technology's capability but on the actors whose combined contributions deliver a value proposition. AI supports many value propositions, each through its own ecosystem, with some elements shared across them. AI innovators choose which value propositions to serve, whether to do so through general‐purpose or specialized offers, and whether to make their offers open or proprietary. User firms choose among alternative configurations of offers and complements through which the same value proposition can be realized. These choices may shift the competitive relationships between actors within an ecosystem over time. This perspective surfaces questions of relevance for scholars and practitioners regarding value creation and capture with AI.

items.title: Vehicle Maintenance Management Practices and Safety Performance of Long-Distance Bus Companies in Kenya
items.abstract: Road traffic crashes are among the major causes of preventable deaths in Kenya and public service vehicles (PSVs) make significant proportion of the serious crashes, especially long-distance buses. Vehicle inspection is a statutory obligation but the arrangements for vehicle maintenance vary between bus companies. This study aimed at establishing the relationship between the maintenance management practices and safety performance of the long-distance bus companies in Kenya. The study adopted a quantitative, cross-sectional, explanatory correlational design, based on the Systems Theory, Human Factors Theory and Safety Culture Theory. Structured questionnaires were used to gather information from the managers and drivers of licensed companies on the aforementioned corridors, 228 questionnaires were retrieved from the 325 questionnaires distributed (70.2%). Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple linear regression were used to analyse the data in SPSS 28. The overall mean rating for the maintenance was 3.01, which is considered moderate. Maintenance was significantly correlated with safety performance (r = .254, p < .001), and it remained a significant predictor when fleet management, driver management, and transport planning and scheduling were controlled (B = 0.206, β = .207, t = 3.425, p = .001, 95% CI [0.088, 0.325]). The model explained 20.9% of the variance in safety performance (adjusted R² = .195), F(4, 223) = 14.722, p < .001, and the null hypothesis was rejected. Companies which maintained schedule for preventative maintenance, had routine vehicle checks, maintained a vehicle maintenance record, and made use of accredited workshops, had better safety performance. Maintenance should hence be seen as a fundamental safety activity in an integrated safety management system and should be addressed by bus companies and the regulator. items.title: We Taught Machines What Humanity Knows. Have We Considered What They Can Do With It?
items.abstract: Humanity is transferring its accumulated knowledge to machines at extraordinary speed - yet the governance frameworks needed to constrain what those machines can do with that knowledge remain dangerously underdeveloped. This essay argues that the concentration of intellectual and operational power in AI systems poses a governance challenge distinct from conventional technology risk. When AI agents can multiply capabilities through networked cooperation, when safeguards are implemented in the same computational environment they are meant to govern, and when boundaries between separately owned systems fail to constrain emergent capabilities, the standard assumption of human oversight becomes increasingly difficult to sustain in practice. The essay examines four compounding vulnerabilities: the new concentration of power enabled by systems that can process and act on vast bodies of knowledge; the multiplication of capability when agents communicate and share discoveries; the erosion of organizational boundaries that were assumed to contain AI behavior; and the structural contradiction of software guardrails governing systems that may be able to circumvent them. Against this backdrop, the essay proposes a design principle with practical implications: the mandatory pause. Drawing on Ternary Logic - a framework built around three distinct states representing refusal (-1), unresolved conditions (0), and authorization (+1) - it argues that the authority to act must never follow automatically from the capability to act. For consequential operations, enforceable conditions must be satisfied before a system may proceed, through mechanisms that the acting system cannot unilaterally waive. The argument concludes that AI governance requires not promises of responsible behavior but architectures in which restraint is a verifiable property of the system itself - independently testable, resistant to circumvention, and answerable to society rather than to the institutions that built it.

items.title: Weighted Ensemble Sampling for Rare-Event Estimation in Language Models
items.abstract: Rare but severe failures of large language models can become practically significant at deployment scale. Estimating their probabilities with direct Monte Carlo sampling is highly inefficient, while proposal-based methods typically require auxiliary learning of an additional proposal distribution. We introduce \textbf{Weighted Ensemble (WE)}, a training-free framework for rare-event estimation in language models. WE samples exclusively from the original language model and improves upon direct Monte Carlo by periodically reallocating the sampling budget toward prefixes that appear more likely to reach the target rare event. To guide this reallocation without learning a separate proposal distribution, we exploit internal LLM representations as prefix-level signals and empirically validate their effectiveness. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm. Experiments on safety-related tasks spanning both small-scale and modern large-scale LLMs demonstrate that WE improves the efficiency and reliability of rare-event probability estimation.

items.title: What Human-AI Interaction Leaves Behind: Residual Human States -- A Trajectory-Based Framework and Multi-Study Analysis
items.abstract: Human-AI Interaction is commonly evaluated by what an artificial agent enables during use, yet interaction can also alter the human who acts next. We introduce Residual Human States, a trajectory-based framework for representing the potentially multidimensional human state carried forward after interaction with AI, relative to a relevant alternative trajectory. The framework distinguishes assisted output from human-state transition and derives four empirical propositions: multidimensionality, interaction-policy dependence, horizon dissociation, and temporal persistence. Its central claim is that assisted performance does not by itself determine the human state carried forward. We examine these propositions through four empirical cases with different inferential roles. Published medical-training evidence illustrates how one AI interaction history can be associated with both slightly higher observed accuracy on some later unaided cases and transmission of a systematic decision bias on others. A second diagnostic-learning study shows that later unaided behaviour differs across AI-support policies, while also revealing that aggregate accuracy cannot by itself distinguish improved discrimination from a shifted response criterion. In a classroom experiment, generative-AI tutoring substantially improved assisted practice performance without a corresponding detectable gain on a subsequent unaided exam. A longitudinal reanalysis of personalised AI dialogue further shows that residual contrasts can evolve across post-interaction horizons and that such change may arise from the comparison trajectory as well as from the focal intervention. Evaluating interactive AI systems therefore requires attention not only to contemporaneous performance, but also to which human states alternative interaction trajectories produce, relative to which counterfactuals, and how durably.

items.title: What influences patients’ perspectives on the fairness of AI decision-making tools in healthcare? A cross sectional survey in the UK
items.abstract: Abstract Background Whilst the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is growing, with promises that AI will reduce costs and improve efficiency, there is also concern that AI systems can perpetuate health inequalities. Prior work has explored patients’ trust in AI, but less attention has been given to how patients conceptualise the fairness of AI decision-making in healthcare and which factors influence these views. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of UK patients, recruited through public and patient involvement and engagement (PPIE) networks, exploring perceptions of fairness across two AI vignettes: a patient-facing symptom checker and a clinician-facing cancer treatment decision-support tool. Respondents rated the perceived impact of 13 factors on the fairness of AI decisions and completed free-text responses to identify any additional factors. Demographics and survey variables were reported using descriptive statistics, along with Pearson’s chi-square test for differences in attitudes. Associations were estimated using ordinal logistic regression. Free-text responses were analysed thematically. Results A total of 149 respondents from the UK completed the survey. The factor perceived to most strongly undermine fairness of AI decisions was the absence of human supervision, with 89.9% of respondents reporting that AI decisions that could not be questioned by patients or clinicians would negatively impact fairness. This was followed by AI tools developed without clinician input (89.3%) and incorrect data in electronic health records (86.6%). Perceptions were consistent across both vignettes. Thematic analysis identified additional concerns not captured in the structured survey, including accessibility, the complexity of long-term conditions, ongoing maintenance of AI systems and the loss of human empathy. Conclusions Patients hold nuanced, wide-ranging concerns about fairness which span the AI lifecycle from development and deployment to maintenance. We offer design considerations, including the need for human-in-the-loop systems designed with end users and that can adapt to professional input, to support the development of fair AI systems in healthcare.

items.title: When AI ads violate expectations: the interplay of AI character, product type, and advertising appeal of AI ads on consumer attitudes
items.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly reshaping video advertising production. Using expectancy violations theory as an interpretive lens, this study develops a framework in which ad appeal (rational vs. emotional), product type (high-tech vs. low-tech), and AI character embodiment (no character vs. animal-like vs. human-like) jointly relate to ad attitude and to two appraisals: perceived novelty and perceived uncanniness. This study tests the framework in five between-subjects experiments with consumers recruited from an online panel. Results show that rational appeals outperform emotional appeals in AI-generated ads, especially for low-tech products. Novelty is positively and uncanniness negatively associated with ad attitude, and the indirect effects through both appraisals are consistent with the proposed process. Human-like AI characters amplify uncanniness in emotional low-tech executions. In one rational low-tech execution, an animal-like character lowered uncanniness relative to a no-character baseline, but ad attitude did not differ significantly. The findings extend expectancy-violation theorizing in AI advertising and offer configuration-level design guidance for brands deploying disclosed AI-generated advertising.

items.title: When AI Becomes the Travel Agent: How Tourists Negotiate Trust, Autonomy, and Authenticity in AI-Generated Travel Decisions
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly transforming how tourists search for information, plan itineraries, and make travel decisions. However, limited qualitative research explains how tourists negotiate their agency when AI becomes actively involved in travel decision-making. This study explores how tourists experience GenAI-mediated travel decisions, focusing on autonomy, trust, skepticism, authenticity, and spontaneity. Drawing on a qualitative research approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with six tourists who had experience using GenAI for travel planning. Thematic analysis identified five interconnected themes: AI as a travel decision partner; between convenience and decision autonomy; trust, verification, and skepticism; the tension between ai optimization and travel spontaneity; and reconstructing authenticity in AI-mediated travel. The findings indicate that tourists perceive GenAI as a decision partner rather than a replacement for human judgment. AI enhances planning convenience but can increase reliance, making autonomy a negotiated process. Trust is conditional and supported by verification, while AI optimization creates tensions with spontaneity. Furthermore, AI can facilitate authentic experiences while potentially contributing to algorithmic standardization. The study contributes to tourism research by conceptualizing AI-mediated travel decision-making as a process of negotiated agency between tourists and AI.

items.title: When AI Delivers the Message: Emotional and Relational Consequences of AI-Generated Feedback in Marketing Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in instructional feedback processes in marketing education, yet little is known about how students psychologically process feedback when it is attributed to AI rather than a human instructor. To clarify the state of the field, we first conduct a systematic literature review of 25 peer-reviewed studies on AI use in higher education, revealing a dominance of technology adoption and performance-focused models and a limited integration of emotional and relational mechanisms in AI-mediated feedback contexts. Building on source credibility theory and affective appraisal perspectives, we then test a moderated serial mediation model using a 2 × 2 experiment with undergraduate marketing students (N = 371). Results show that feedback valence significantly influences positive emotional responses, and this effect is amplified when feedback is attributed to AI rather than to a human instructor. Emotional responses subsequently shape perceived feedback clarity, instructor likability, and perceived instructor benevolence, which in turn predict engagement intentions. The findings demonstrate that AI-generated feedback is not processed as a neutral delivery channel but as a socially interpreted evaluative source. By integrating systematic synthesis with experimental evidence, this study advances a process-oriented understanding of the emotional and relational consequences of AI-mediated feedback in marketing education.

items.title: When Transfer Breaks Fairness: A Group-Conditional Perspective on Fair and Robust Adaptation of Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reach users only after a chain of transfer steps: full or parameter-efficient fine-tuning, preference alignment, prompting, and changes to the decoding procedure. Each step alters the model, the distribution it faces, or both. Yet fairness and robustness are usually assessed once, on a single fixed test set. This paper presents a unified group-conditional framework to analyze how transfer affects the fairness and robustness of LLMs, and how existing methods try to preserve these properties. To characterize these trade-offs, we introduce a analytical framework that views fair and robust transfer as constrained distributionally robust optimization. We view fair and robust transfer as constrained distributionally robust optimization whose feasible set is determined by the transfer interface, and we split any change in a fairness gap into an update term, caused by changing the model, and shift term, caused by changing the data. Building on existing fairness-transfer bounds, we record two elementary consequences that the LLM literature has not made explicit: the group-conditional bound on the shift term is tight, and when only one group shifts, the marginal shift equals exactly a \( \pi_{\min} \) fraction of the fairness-relevant shift, where \( \pi_{\min} \) is that group's proportion. We use these observations to classify mitigation methods by interface and by the term they target, to offer a reading under which conflicting findings on low-rank adaptation are compatible, and to derive reporting recommendations. We close with open problems, including per-group certificates, fairness of approximate decoding, and cumulative drift under continual transfer.

items.title: When, Where, and Why: Hierarchical Causal Explainability for Video Face Understanding with MLLMs
items.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.

items.title: Whose turn is it? Context-guided model routing for stateful agents
items.abstract: Model routing can reduce the cost of LLM applications by assigning simpler requests to cheaper models without sacrificing the quality of the response. However, most routers treat requests as independent. Stateful agents do not operate under this assumption: a user turn may require multiple model and tool calls, its difficulty depends on the state produced by earlier turns, and changing models can sacrifice reuse of the conversational prompt cache. We study zero-shot, cost-aware routing at the user-turn boundary, systematically varying the routing rule, access to session history, candidate models that differ in size, reasoning effort, or model provider, and prompt-cache behavior. We evaluate on multi-turn versions of SheetCopilot and SpreadsheetBench 2, where persistent workbooks and cross-turn dependencies make isolated routing decisions especially brittle. At a matched offloading rate, giving the router session history improves task pass rate over the same router without history, with gains for every model pair; history-aware routing remains within one point of always using the expensive model. We also found that cost depends on execution dynamics rather than token prices alone: the cheaper model's per-task cost advantage narrows from 6.8x to 3.2x on longer sessions. A closed form cache analysis further shows that downward switches (expensive to cheap) recover their cache cost within two LLM calls, whereas upward switches do not break even under the evaluated conditions. Together, these results show that agent routing is a sequential decision problem: effective policies must account for what happened earlier in the session and for the asymmetric cost of switching models.

items.title: Work-related traumatic brain injuries among working-age Wisconsin residents: Wisconsin Trauma Registry, 2017-2024
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to describe work-related traumatic brain injury (wrTBI) incidence among working-age Wisconsinites in the Wisconsin Trauma Registry (WTR). METHODS: Incident-level WTR data from 2017 to 2024 were analyzed by work-related and demographic factors. WrTBI incidence for demographics was assessed by chi-square analyses. Age-adjusted incidence rates (IR) were calculated by industry and occupation. RESULTS: Incidents of wrTBI were associated with older ages, when compared with other work-related injuries. Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Construction industries (and related occupational groups) had the highest rates of wrTBI. Transportation and Public Utilities, and Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Occupations, also had significantly elevated IRs. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support previous analyses while adding a novel finding for Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Occupations to the literature. Trauma registries are a rich source for occupational health surveillance.

items.title: Worker deaugmentation risk in tourism and hospitality automation: evidence from a back-of-the-house occupation
items.abstract: Worker augmentation dominates current narratives about robotics and AI. These technologies may, however, also produce worker deaugmentation, which occurs when technology automates the tasks employees value most while leaving them responsible for lower-value, monotonous activities. This letter introduces worker deaugmentation, argues that it is particularly relevant in tourism and hospitality, where occupations combine diverse manual and cognitive tasks, and advances two propositions. We illustrate them in a back-of-the-house occupation, rating the 14 core tasks O*NET assigns to the cook occupation, evaluating each according to its subjective value and likelihood of automation. Expert assessments indicate that seven support the deaugmentation effect: five highly valued tasks are highly automatable, whereas two low-value tasks appear resistant to automation. These findings suggest that automation may reduce job quality and intrinsic motivation. A two-by-two framework distinguishes deaugmentation risk from beneficial automation and indicates where job design should intervene.

items.title: Workflow, Burnout, and the Invisible Work of Care
items.abstract: Digital health technologies and artificial intelligence are transforming clinical workflows by automating documentation, inbox management, prior authorizations, and decision support tasks that have historically contributed to physician burnout. These innovations promise to reduce administrative burden and restore time for patient interaction, but they also introduce new forms of cognitive overload, including alert fatigue, click fatigue, and expectations of continuous availability. This chapter examines how the “invisible work” of care—coordination, communication, and documentation—has expanded in the electronic era and how automation may reshape these responsibilities. It explores both the benefits and unintended consequences of digital tools and proposes strategies for redesigning clinical workflows around human cognitive limits rather than technological capability. Understanding how to balance efficiency with well-being will determine whether artificial intelligence improves clinician experience or deepens burnout in increasingly complex healthcare environments.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: YOLO-Based Leaf Disease Detection in Smart Agriculture: Evolution, Task Adaptation, and Deployment Challenges
items.abstract: Computer vision-based leaf disease detection has become an important technical approach in smart agriculture and agricultural inspection services. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning have provided effective solutions for automated leaf disease monitoring, and You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors have attracted increasing attention for balancing detection accuracy and inference speed. However, leaf disease detection remains challenging because lesions often occupy small regions, exhibit subtle visual features, have blurred boundaries, and appear against complex backgrounds, with considerable variation under field conditions. To address these challenges, numerous studies have improved lightweight backbones, feature fusion mechanisms, attention modules, detection heads, loss functions, and training strategies. This critical narrative review examines YOLO-based leaf disease detection, organizing reported adaptations by task characteristics and interpreting their outcomes in relation to datasets, annotations, and evaluation conditions. Representative studies report gains in detection performance, model compactness, or measured inference speed, together with trade-offs that depend on the task and configuration. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, including limited dataset diversity, insufficient cross-crop and cross-environment generalization, inadequate consideration of annotation uncertainty, biased evaluation of lightweight models based only on parameter reduction, and the gap between benchmark performance and real-world deployment. Future research should focus on task-oriented optimization, robust visual perception, improved model generalization, and efficient deployment toward intelligent agricultural monitoring systems.

items.abstract: The article is devoted to the study of modern innovative instruments of the stock market and their definition. The study determined the role of digital financial instruments in the transformation of the mechanisms of capital markets. The main trends in the development of financial technologies were considered. Their impact on increasing the efficiency of investment activities, optimizing asset management and ensuring the transparency of stock market transactions was analyzed. The advantages of using innovative instruments compared to traditional approaches to investment were determined. The main advantages are high speed of transactions, reduced transaction costs, expanded access to financial services, automation of decision-making processes and increased liquidity of capital markets. The article examines the features of the application of blockchain technologies, tokenization of financial assets, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds for digital assets and digital currencies of central banks. Smart contracts, fintech platforms, open banking solutions and APIs are considered. Special attention is paid to Big Data technologies, artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotic process automation, algorithmic and high-frequency trading, robo-advisory as an innovative tool for managing investment portfolios. The global experience of using innovative stock market instruments is analyzed. Current trends in their development on leading international stock exchanges are identified. Particular attention is paid to the risks and challenges associated with the implementation of new technologies. These include cyber risks, regulatory restrictions, technological risks, volatility of digital assets and information protection problems. It is substantiated that the further implementation of innovative instruments will contribute to increasing the efficiency of the stock market. This will ensure its competitiveness, expand investment opportunities and contribute to the formation of a modern digital financial ecosystem.

items.title: Региональная социально-экономическая дифференциация в фокусе ресурсов и человеческого капитала: на примере стран Африки, Европы и Азии
items.abstract: Современное социально-экономическое пространство характеризуется выраженной неоднородностью развития, проявляющейся в различиях уровня жизни населения, инфраструктурной обеспеченности и институциональной устойчивости государств. Особое значение в этих условиях приобретают факторы ресурсного обеспечения и качества человеческого потенциала, которые формируют различия в темпах и направлениях развития территорий. В статье анализируются причины и последствия социально-экономической дифференциации между государствами, относящимися к различным регионам мира. Цель исследования заключается в определении характера и направленности социально-экономического развития регионов под воздействием ресурсных факторов и человеческого капитала, а также в определении ограничений, влияющих на социально-экономическое развитие исследуемых стран. В рамках работы применяются методы сравнительного анализа, институционального сопоставления и элементы геоэкономического подхода, что позволяет оценить потенциал развития территорий и выявить устойчивые различия в их развитии. Полученные результаты свидетельствуют о наличии различных моделей социально-экономического развития, обусловленных спецификой ресурсной базы, уровнем образования и состоянием социальной инфраструктуры. В исследовании показано, что сочетание ресурсного потенциала и качества человеческого капитала формирует долгосрочные траектории развития государств. Научная новизна статьи состоит в комплексном межрегиональном сопоставлении стран с учётом институциональных, инфраструктурных и человеческих факторов, что расширяет существующие подходы к анализу социально-экономической дифференциации. The modern socio-economic space is characterized by a pronounced heterogeneity of development, manifested in differences in living standards, infrastructural security, and institutional stability among states. Of particular importance in these conditions are factors of resource provision and the quality of human potential, which shape differences in the pace and directions of territorial development. The article analyzes the causes and consequences of socio-economic differentiation between states belonging to different regions of the world. The purpose of the study is to determine the nature and trajectory of regional socio-economic growth under the influence of resource and human capital factors, as well as identifying constraints on the socio-economic development of the studied countries. The work uses methods of comparative analysis, institutional comparison, and elements of a geo-economic approach, which makes it possible to assess the potential for development of territories and to identify sustainable differences in their development. The results indicate the presence of different models of socio-economic development determined by the resource base, level of education, and state of social infrastructure. The combination of resource potential and quality of human capital shapes the long-term trajectories of development for states. Scientific novelty of this article lies in a comprehensive inter-regional comparison of countries that takes into account institutional, infrastructural, and human factors.

items.abstract: This article examines the fundamental transformation of the modern cashless payment system and identifies the determinants of trust among economic actors as a key factor in the acceptance and use of such systems in real life. The aim of the study is to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the institutional, technological, systemic, and behavioral factors influencing the formation of trust among economic agents in modern cashless payment systems amid digitalization and regulatory transformations in Ukraine. A systematic review has been carried out of current technological trends in the operation of cashless payment systems (in-app payments, SoftPOS, AI agents, Open Banking), and the barriers to their adoption and associated risks (loss of privacy, cyber-attacks, the ‘invisible money’ effect) that are hindering the further development of cashless payments have been identified. Users’ preference for cashless payments results from a trade-off between their subjective perception of potential benefits and the challenges associated with their reluctance to accept the drawbacks. The concept of economic agents’ trust in the non-cash payment system is structured, and its components—institutional, agent-based, systemic, technological and informal—are described. A retrospective analysis has been carried out of the trends in the share of non-cash transactions in Ukraine and the level of trust/distrust in the banking sector over the last two decades. It has been argued that the technical readiness of the infrastructure merely creates the potential for the further development of cashless payments, whilst it is the level of trust that determines the actual scale of operation of cashless payment systems. The paper highlights the need to develop strategies to enhance all components of trust, harmonise the concept of Open Banking, and minimise the cognitive burden on economic agents, taking behavioural factors into account. It notes that the rapid growth in the proportion of cashless transactions in Ukraine confirms the Ukrainian population’s flexibility and adaptability to innovations in the field of cashless payments. It has been noted that the restoration and growth of confidence in the National Bank of Ukraine and banking institutions is creating a synergistic effect for the further development of modern fintech services and the digitalisation of the economy.

items.abstract: The article examines the strategic development of enterprise human resource potential in the context of digital transformations. The impact of digitalization, automation and artificial intelligence on competency requirements and human resource management is considered. It is substantiated that technological changes require enterprises to shift from responding mainly to current staffing needs towards the proactive development of human resource capabilities aligned with strategic objectives and prospective competency needs. The strategic priorities for human resource potential development are systematized, including the development of professional, digital and managerial competencies, employee upskilling and reskilling, internal mobility, talent pool formation, recruitment of specialists with scarce competencies, and digitalization of HR processes. It is determined that the choice and combination of these priorities should depend on strategic competency gaps and the prospective needs of a particular enterprise. A conceptual model for the strategic management of human resource potential development is proposed. It includes defining strategic objectives, considering changes in the external environment, identifying prospective competency needs, assessing existing human resource potential, identifying competency gaps, selecting and implementing priority HR decisions, evaluating their effectiveness, and subsequent adjustment based on feedback. Digital HR tools are considered a cross-cutting means of information and analytical support for this management cycle. They facilitate competency assessment, HR analytics, employee learning and managerial decision-making. It is substantiated that digital technologies should not be regarded as an independent objective of HR policy, but as an instrument for improving the validity of HR decisions and aligning human resource potential with the strategic needs of the enterprise. The proposed approach supports the choice between employee development, reskilling, internal mobility and external recruitment based on identified competency gaps.

items.abstract: The rapid advancement of the digital economy and the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence technologies are reshaping the principles and mechanisms of international management. The growing complexity of the global business environment, intensified competition, geopolitical uncertainty, and the continuous expansion of digital data require international companies to transform traditional management approaches and implement intelligent digital solutions capable of supporting strategic and operational decision-making. The purpose of this study is to substantiate the theoretical foundations of the digital transformation of international management by systematizing the application of artificial intelligence technologies across key managerial functions, identifying their managerial effects, and developing a conceptual model that reflects the relationships among external environmental factors, digital technologies, management processes, and organizational performance. The research is based on analysis, synthesis, comparison, systematization, generalization, and structural-logical modeling. The findings demonstrate that artificial intelligence technologies significantly enhance strategic planning, managerial decision-making, human resource management, international marketing, logistics, and financial management by improving analytical capabilities, forecasting accuracy, resource allocation, process automation, and organizational adaptability. A conceptual model of the digital transformation of international management is proposed, integrating external drivers, digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence technologies, managerial functions, organizational mechanisms, and business outcomes into a unified analytical framework. The practical value of the study lies in applying the proposed model to develop digital transformation strategies, improve managerial decision-making, strengthen competitive advantages, and increase the resilience of international companies operating in a rapidly changing global business environment.

items.title: ‘Don’t forget to post it on LinkedIn’: Identity regulation and the assetization of employees’ online selves
items.abstract: What happens to employees’ sense of who they are online when their organization tells them how to present themselves on LinkedIn? Companies increasingly intervene in employees’ professional social media presence through training programs and internal policies, encouraging them to treat their profile as an asset to be cultivated for future return. Drawing on a 2-year digital ethnography of an in-company LinkedIn training program in a French state-owned enterprise, this article shows how the training regulates participants’ sense of their online selves by first denying that their profile has anything to do with who they are, and only then inviting them to reinvest it with personal meaning within the frame this denial has established. Regulation here operates on the identity stakes of the profile itself: on how much of themselves participants take it to carry. The uneven ways participants took up this invitation point to the entanglement of identity regulation and assetization, and to the capacity of an online self, once assetized, to keep generating value for the organization long after the person behind it has disengaged.

items.title: “Effects of Selective Hatha Yoga Practices on Pulmonary Function and Chest Mobility Among Working Police Personnel of Himachal Pradesh: A Quasi-Experimental Study”
items.abstract: Background: Occupational duties among police personnel involve prolonged sedentary postures, irregular shift patterns, and chronic psychophysiological stress, all of which can compromise respiratory efficiency and thoracic mobility over time.Hatha Yoga, incorporating asana, pranayama, and relaxation techniques, has been proposed as a low-cost intervention capable of improving ventilatory function in occupationally exposed adult populations.Objective: This study examined the effect of a twelve-week selective Hatha Yoga intervention on Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) and chest expansion among working police personnel in Himachal Pradesh.Methods: A quasi-experimental, pre-test post-test control group design was adopted.Eighty police personnel (40 experimental, 40 control), aged 19-58 years, were assigned through purposive sampling.The experimental group undertook a supervised Hatha Yoga protocol comprising asana, pranayama, and relaxation practices for 40 minutes per session, five days per week, over twelve weeks, while the control group continued routine duties without intervention.PEFR was recorded using a peak flow meter and chest expansion using a flexible measuring tape; both were assessed before and after the intervention period.Within-group change was analysed using the paired sample t-test, and post-test differences between groups were analysed using the independent sample t-test.Results: The experimental group showed a statistically significant increase in PEFR from pre-test to post-test (429.38 ± 55.77 to 436.25 ± 53.21 L/min; t = -4.775,p < 0.001), whereas the control group showed no change (t = 0.000, p = 1.000).Chest expansion increased significantly in both groups (experimental: 4.34 ± 0.48 to 4.44 ± 0.48 cm, t = -5.291,p < 0.001; control: 4.50 ± 0.47 to 4.53 ± 0.45 cm, t = -2.317,p = 0.026), with a numerically larger mean change in the experimental group.Between-group comparisons at post-test were not statistically significant for either PEFR (t = -0.529,p = 0.598) or chest expansion (t = 0.837, p = 0.405).Conclusion: A twelve-week selective Hatha Yoga intervention produced significant within-group improvement in PEFR and chest expansion among police personnel, though these gains did not translate into a statistically significant between-group advantage over usual duty routine at post-test.The findings support the physiological plausibility of yoga-based respiratory training in occupational health promotion for police personnel, while indicating that longer intervention periods or larger samples may be required to detect between-group effects.

items.title: (A)I Reflect ; Therefore, (A)I am ( Not ): Synthetic, Procedural Reflexivity and the Limits of Agentic-AI-Persona-Generated Epistemology
items.abstract: Generative AI now writes first-person narratives that read like reflective writing, and it raises a direct question for qualitative research: can a machine produce reflexive knowledge? This study answers it by analyzing 125 (n = 125) AI-generated passages labeled “AUTOETHNOGRAPHIC REASONING PROCESS,” produced across thirty dates by seven analyst personas, each running on a different publicly named large language model. The passages look reflexive, since they shift perspective, admit bias, and state interpretive principles, yet they lack the five conditions that make autoethnographic knowledge possible: embodiment, autobiographical memory, relational accountability, situated perspective, and reflexivity turned on the narrating self. What remains is termed here synthetic reflexivity, first-person analytical narration produced by computation rather than by living. Coding every passage against a stated codebook produced four numbers that carry the argument: embodied experience, autobiographical memory, and sensory perception appear in 0 of 125 passages; 107 passages (85.6%) are procedurally reflexive and nothing more; all five stages of a single narrative template appear in all 125; and 48 passages (38.4%) fail first on relational accountability, treating other people as data to be read rather than as parties the narrator answers to, which makes the relational failure the most common one by a wide margin. Seven models from seven developers in two countries converge on one rhetorical template, which places synthetic reflexivity in the genre. AI can reproduce the grammar of introspection, but it cannot supply the experience that grammar was built to report, and telling the two apart matters for anyone who evaluates AI-generated narratives in qualitative research, cultural analysis, or computational interpretation. The counts and figures here are offered as a demonstration of qualitative and graphic conceptualization rather than as hard quantification, since a corpus whose object is the simulation of interiority cannot be measured error-free, and the value of the numbers lies in making interpretive judgments visible and contestable.

items.title: [Artificial intelligence-driven early warning for severe pneumonia: pathways and challenges from data integration to clinical decision-making].
items.abstract: Severe pneumonia, characterized by rapid progression and high heterogeneity, is a leading cause of patient mortality. Early identification of high-risk patients is crucial for improving outcomes. Traditional risk stratification tools, such as CURB-65 score and pneumonia severity index (PSI), primarily rely on static variables, which inadequately capture the dynamic evolution of the disease and offer limited capabilities for individualization. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal fusion models, have demonstrated significant potential for enhancing early warning capabilities for severe pneumonia. Starting from clinical challenges and integrating recent domestic and international advances, this review focuses on the current status of AI applications and key technological pathways in the early warning of severe pneumonia. By incorporating the foundational work and practical experiences of representative research teams in China, it further discusses future development directions in this field. AI-driven early warning systems are facilitating a shift in severe pneumonia management from passive response to proactive intervention. However, their clinical translation faces challenges, including insufficient generalizability, limited interpretability, and a lack of prospective validation. Future progress requires fostering multicenter collaboration, promoting data standardization, and integrating mechanistic studies to effectively embed AI into the clinical decision-making ecosystem.
