items.title: A correlational study of animation narrative style preferences, viewing behavior, and audience experience
items.abstract: Introduction The association between animation narrative styles and the audience’s psychological experience is a critical question in media psychology. Grounded in Uses and Gratifications (U&G), this cross-sectional correlational study examines how narrative preferences are associated with viewing experience. Methods Through a survey of 615 animation viewers, we evaluated how complex/non-linear, coherent/linear, and visual/expressive preferences correlate with cognitive engagement and flow experience. K-Means cluster analysis was utilized for audience segmentation. Results Two significant “preference-experience” pathways emerged: a positive correlation between a preference for complexity and cognitive engagement, and a strong correlation between a preference for coherence and flow experience. Furthermore, viewers were clustered into Analytical Viewers, Casual Plot-Followers, and Indifferent Viewers. Cognitive engagement exhibited a statistical indirect association between complexity preference and flow experience. Discussion These findings supply empirical evidence for understanding audience selection behaviors and offer evidence-bounded implications for content creation and platform recommendation strategies, highlighting an eudaimonic and a hedonic gratification path.

items.title: A cross-sectional study on the mental health status and influencing factors of medical staff in northwestern China
items.abstract: Healthcare workers in Northwest China face heavy workloads and limited resources, yet region-specific evidence on their health is scarce. In this multicentre cross-sectional study, 1143 doctors, nurses and other clinical staff from 151 public hospitals in Northwest China were surveyed in November–December 2023 using a questionnaire compiled from existing Chinese instruments that assessed occupational stressors, mental health, chronic physical diseases and body image. Nearly 60% of participants worked more than five days per week. Longer daily working hours and more weekly working days were independently associated with greater psychological distress, although the model explained only a small proportion of the variance. Staff in secondary hospitals and non-provincial capital cities reported greater psychological distress than those in tertiary hospitals and provincial capitals. Physical diseases were more common among men, emergency department staff and those working longer hours. Physical exertion was the most prominent stressor, followed by psychological and economic stress, and doctors reported higher stress levels than nurses. These findings suggest that workload management, mental health support and occupational health policies targeting high-risk groups may help to protect the well-being of healthcare workers in this region.

items.title: A Hybrid Agentic RAG Architecture with Knowledge Graphs and Text-to-SQL for Automating Citizen Services in a Public Scientific Institution
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible but incorrect content, a risk that is unacceptable when public institutions disclose scientific and legal information. This study presents and evaluates a hybrid agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that automates first-level responses to citizen information requests at the Marine Institute of Peru (IMARPE). A baseline analysis of 196 requests showed a mean response time of 12 business days, above the 10-day legal limit, and identified 26.9% of them as routine, data-extractable queries. The system, developed under CRISP-DM, uses LangGraph to route each query to a LightRAG knowledge graph (Neo4j) built from institutional yearbooks, to a Text-to-SQL agent that queries the IMARSIS relational database through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or to both, with Gemini 2.5 Flash as the foundation model and a referral protocol for out-of-scope requests. Five institutional domain experts rated 30 test cases, with mean scores of 4.45/5 for factual accuracy, 4.10/5 for completeness, and 4.57/5 for clarity. Mean end-to-end software latency was 20.43 s (maximum 49.20 s), and 30 pilot users rated usability at 80.42 on the System Usability Scale (Cronbach’s α = 0.96). These preliminary, single-site results indicate that combining graph-based and SQL-based grounding is feasible for routine citizen-information services; comparison with simpler baselines remains pending.

items.title: A Model of Human-Automation Team Performance: Incorporating the Influence of Concurrent Task Workload on Automation Failure Response in Ground Vehicles
items.abstract: We first present a model of the influence of four properties of automation on human-automation team performance, dichotomized between conditions when automation functions as designed and when automation fails. These properties are reliability, transparency, degree of automation, and concurrent task workload during automation use. Mediating cognitive variables between properties and performance are trust, dependence, situation awareness, and mental workload. The strength of these influences is estimated from effect sizes in meta-analyses. We then present a meta-analysis of the effect of concurrent task workload on automation failure response as a function of non-driving related task (NDRT) workload within the context of driver take-over request time. Results from 11 studies revealed no overall penalties (mean effect size) for workload on failure response but found considerable variability across studies. Possible moderator variables, including task engagement are presented. These results are interpreted in terms of a model of optimal resource allocation between monitoring automation and the NDRT.

items.title: A Narrative-Driven, Socratic Instructional Framework for Teaching Adversarial Cognition in Cybersecurity
items.abstract: The Socratic method has demonstrated, in studies across law, medicine, and nursing, that dialectic structured questioning improves expert reasoning. Cybersecurity currently teaches tools and techniques but lacks Socratic dialogic leaving graduates underprepared for novel scenarios requiring cross-domain reasoning. Because law, medicine and nursing cultivate similar reasoning as security there is principled reason to expect reasoning benefits could transfer to security students. This paper argues that the correspondence warrants investigation. Investigation requires a named, teachable reasoning target analogous to clinical reasoning and we specify that target as adversarial cognition, a framework integrating adversary features, system architecture, implementation logic, governance structure, human factors, and systemic entropy into attack or defense pathways. These five echo the causal analysis of the Socratic and Aristotelian tradition and modern failure analysis in engineering, information security, and quality management. Our method adapts the Socratic elenchus as nursing and legal education have, pairing questioning with narration and productive misdirection. We evaluate the method to cognitive apprenticeship, situated learning, and narrative pedagogy, demonstrate it through a documented Active Directory attack case, and specify an open, replicable protocol testing whether Socratic-trained practitioners differ from procedurally trained students. The protocol is designed to reveal whether Socratic training improves domain-specific reasoning, general reasoning, or both. Finally, because the same measurement applies to LLM reasoning, we propose comparing Socratic student reasoning and LLM reasoning now that AI-assisted offensive tools make understanding differences in adversarial reasoning increasingly consequential.

items.title: A neuro-symbolic clinical decision support system for chronic pain management using structured derivation traces, adaptive compute, and knowledge graph constraint checking: comparison with 30 physicians from pain-relevant specialties
items.abstract: Chronic pain management requires complex multidisciplinary reasoning integrating pharmacological, interventional, rehabilitative, and psychosocial approaches across multiple guideline frameworks (International Association for the Study of Pain [IASP], American College of Rheumatology [ACR], European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology [EULAR], American Academy of Neurology [AAN], American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine [ASRA], and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [CDC]). Large language models (LLMs) show promise in clinical reasoning but lack any mechanism that records whether encoded guideline criteria were matched, are susceptible to hallucination, and cannot provide auditable decision chains—critical limitations where polypharmacy risks, opioid safety, and nuanced pain mechanism classification (nociplastic vs. nociceptive vs. neuropathic) demand the highest decision rigor. Some classical neuro-symbolic (NS) systems offer formal guarantees, yet such systems are heterogeneous and can lack contextual flexibility. We present PainNS-Prove, a guideline-provable neuro-symbolic clinical decision support system for chronic pain. We evaluate non-inferiority against 30 board-certified physicians from three pain-relevant specialties (10 anesthesiologists and algologists, 10 PM&R specialists, and 10 rheumatologists), all in active chronic pain practice across 30 expert-validated clinical vignettes. The five-stage pipeline integrates Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-4.1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro: (1) multi-LLM structured chain-of-thought with pain-specific prompting, (2) knowledge graph constraint checking against a Neo4j pain ontology (52,418 nodes; 203,672 edges), (3) structured derivation-trace generation with a Lean 4-inspired rule engine, (4) adaptive compute allocation, (5) screening of factual claims via multi-source triangulation, designed to prevent unsupported content from reaching the output. Statistical analyses included non-inferiority testing (δ = 5%), Fleiss’ κ (30 raters), Cohen’s κ (435 pairs), expert variability envelope, inter-specialty ANOVA, error typology with Fisher’s exact tests, ablation with McNemar’s tests, and counterfactual robustness analysis. PainNS-Prove achieved 90.0% accuracy (27/30; 95% CI: 74.4–96.5%), exceeding the expert panel mean of 78.0% (SD = 6.9%). The primary analysis was recomputed with a cluster-aware conservative method based on the 30 rater-level accuracies. The estimated marginal accuracy difference between PainNS-Prove and the expert benchmark was + 12.0% points, with a one-sided 95% lower confidence bound of − 0.7% points. Because this lower bound exceeded the pre-specified margin of − 5% points, non-inferiority was supported (one-sided p = 0.014). The two-sided 95% confidence interval for the difference was − 3.8 to + 19.0% points and includes zero, so superiority was not demonstrated ( p = 0.121) and is not claimed. In sensitivity analyses that modelled the shared vignette structure (vignette-level paired analysis, two-way rater and vignette variance decomposition, vignette-cluster bootstrap), the one-sided 95% lower bound ranged from − 0.8 to 0.0% points, and the non-inferiority conclusion was unchanged. Specialty means: algology 82.3% (SD = 5.0%), PM&R 77.0% (SD = 6.4%), rheumatology 74.7% (SD = 7.2%); inter-specialty ANOVA F(2,27) = 3.93, p = 0.032. The system fell within the expert variability envelope (64.3–91.7%) in 93.3% of cases. Human–human Fleiss’ κ = 0.52 (95% CI: 0.46–0.58); system–expert κ = 0.68 (0.59–0.77). Error typology: 70.7% of human errors were cognitive biases (anchoring 33.3%, availability 22.2%, premature closure 15.2%), 18.2% polypharmacy/opioid safety oversight, 11.1% guideline misapplication. PainNS-Prove produced no errors classified as cognitive bias and none classified as polypharmacy oversight; 3 errors in total (atypical presentation 66.7%, insufficient context 33.3%). Full pipeline outperformed LLM-only by + 16.7% points, which did not reach statistical significance (exact McNemar p = 0.063). Counterfactual stability: 90.0% vs. LLM-only 66.7% ( p = 0.016). PainNS-Prove was non-inferior to a panel of 30 physicians with active chronic pain practice at the pre-specified margin. Among the three incorrect system responses, none was classified by the two adjudicators as cognitive bias or as polypharmacy oversight. Because the number of system errors was small and the taxonomy may classify human errors and system errors differently, no comparative safety inference should be drawn from these counts. These findings come from a single set of 30 vignettes and require multicentre validation before any clinical use.

items.title: A New Lens on Multi-GPU Communication: API-Level Memory Models for Portable Optimization
items.abstract: As network communication increasingly becomes a performance bottleneck for ML and HPC workloads, it is more important than ever to optimize multi-GPU data transfers. Recently, low-level device APIs have emerged that allow programmers to perform fine-grain optimizations via one-sided put/get operations triggered directly from the device. However, the communication libraries providing these device APIs (e.g., rocSHMEM, MSCCL++, and NCCL/RCCL GIN) currently lack a rigorous memory model defining how their primitives interact with the underlying memory systems. Without this, emerging HPC and ML workloads aggressively optimizing network communication via device APIs can be brittle, error-prone, and face compatibility and inter-operability challenges. This paper proposes the use of API-level memory models for these emerging device communication APIs. An API-level memory model defines the memory semantics of communication API calls in a way that abstracts lower-level details from the API user and simplifies development. This work defines one such model for device-side communication (implemented in AMD's recently open sourced rocSHMEM library) and demonstrates how formal relaxations to such a model can enable low-level LLM performance optimizations while retaining a well-defined standardized interface. Specifically, we describe how updating the SHMEM API implemented by rocSHMEM can properly support cache bypassing for network data, improving performance of a collective communication workload by up to 2.48x, a fused compute+communication workload by up to 1.77x, and a state-of-the-art expert-parallel communication workload by up to 1.18x.

items.title: A Novel Image Filtering Approach for Image Classification Applied to Severity Assessment of Root Rot Disease in Arugula Cultivation
items.abstract: In this paper, a new image filtering method is proposed using nonlinear symbolic functions. In this way, feature extraction from images is achieved using a small number of filters and parameters. Nonlinear symbolic functions are determined by an optimization method and different approaches are proposed to increase the filtering speed. Nonlinear functions also act as a regression layer and more efficient design is achieved by moving the image to nonlinear space. In sustainable agriculture, artificial intelligence has been recently utilized to pre-detect diseases and determine their severity to perform spraying more accurately in site-specific applications for human health and soil ingredients. Therefore, a new dataset for detecting the disease root rot severity of Arugula (Eruca vesicaria) was created and labeled for the image classification such that there is a significant decrease in production yield every year due to root rot disease. The proposed CNN model with nonlinear symbolic function filtering was produced %86.92 accuracy for the classification of disease severity whereas conventional 4-layer CNN model and pre-trained large image classification models such as VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, ResNet101, InceptionV3, DenseNet, EfficientNetV2S, MobileNet, MobileNetV2 and Xception have been fine-tuned and classification accuracy is provided between 57-92% without preprocessing of images. Between the designed models, MobileNet model with less computational time and high accuracy can be a potential for future application in drone-based spraying systems. However, the proposed model with less number of parameters is also promising for future applications. The application results of image classification facilitate variable-rate spraying for sustainable agricultural production, ultimately protecting both human and soil health.

items.title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

items.title: A review on advances in chemical compound toxicology prediction
items.abstract: The accurate prediction of chemical toxicity remains a major challenge in drug development and chemical safety assessment because conventional approaches can be costly, time-consuming, ethically constrained, and limited in predictive performance. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is being applied to predictive toxicology. It covers conventional algorithms such as support vector machines (SVMs), decision trees (DTs), and ensemble methods, together with advanced approaches including graph neural networks (GNNs). The review evaluates AI-based methods across five organ-specific toxicity domains—hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, respiratory toxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neurotoxicity—and critically compares molecular representations, data-integration strategies, model architectures, validation protocols, and interpretability approaches. Particular emphasis is placed on data quality, class imbalance, model explainability, applicability domains, external validation, and regulatory acceptance. By integrating recent methodological advances with persistent implementation challenges, this review provides a technical framework for developing more transparent, reliable, and generalizable computational tools for safety assessment in drug discovery and environmental health.

items.title: A Sense of Proprioception in Language Models
items.abstract: In humans, proprioception corresponds to the sense of self-movement or position, e.g. understanding the position of one's arm. This sense is often less well-understood and in popular understanding sometimes conflated with introspection. But, notably, proprioception is a separate sense, with dedicated receptors and verifiable outcomes. On the other hand though, language models cannot observe their own internal states during training (and for example answer the question which experts activated in a certain layer of an MoE) and so cannot accurately report on them. Yet, such information is, by virtue of being internal to the model, both accessible, and readily constructed into verifiable signals. We argue that this provides the basis for a digital analog of proprioception. As such, we train models through SFT and on-policy training to equip them with this ability. We show that modern models can be trained to understand a range of subtypes of proprioception, such as routing decision awareness, token entropy, decision depth or logit lens information, without affecting model capabilities. We then run these models through a broad evaluation of situational awareness, legibility, and epiphenomenality, to evaluate in what ways access to proprioception changes model behavior.

items.title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.

items.title: A Systematic Review of Deepfake Detection Techniques: Cross-Dataset Generalization, Computational Efficiency, And Performance Evaluation
items.abstract: Deepfake technology has emerged as a major challenge to the authenticity and trustworthiness of digital media.The rapid development of artificial intelligence and deep learning has made it possible to generate highly realistic manipulated images, videos, and other forms of digital content.As a result, reliable deepfake detection systems are increasingly important for digital forensics, cybersecurity, social media platforms, and the protection of information integrity.This paper presents a systematic review of deepfake detection techniques published between 2018 and 2025, with particular attention to deep learning, traditional machine learning, and classical image-processing approaches.The review focuses on detection performance, computational efficiency, and cross-dataset generalization.Studies evaluated using FaceForensics++, the DeepFake Detection Challenge (DFDC), and Celeb-DF indicate that Transformer-based methods generally demonstrate stronger cross-dataset generalization than evaluated CNN-based approaches.However, this improved generalization comes with substantially higher computational requirements.Traditional machine learning approaches, particularly Random Forest, can provide competitive performance in some settings while requiring fewer computational resources.Overall, performance degradation of approximately 10-15% across datasets remain a significant challenge.These findings indicate that future deepfake detection research should prioritize robustness, generalization, computational efficiency, and real-world deployment rather than focusing exclusively on accuracy.

items.title: Accountability as Infrastructure: A Design Theory of AI-Enabled Planning Authority
items.abstract: Problem, research strategy, and findings Urban planning agencies are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) faster than they are developing procedures for governing its continued use. In this study I developed and diagnostically applied a design theory for keeping AI-supported planning authority publicly inspectable, challengeable, and withdrawable after deployment. The research went through four stages: identifying recurrent institutional failures documented in planning and public sector AI scholarship; synthesizing six established accountability tools into an integrated institutional design; applying that design diagnostically to Gainesville’s (FL) micromobility program; and deriving six propositions with observable measures and comparative research designs. In this analysis I identified three recurrent risks: unauthorized expansion of system use, weakening oversight, and persistent distributional underperformance. Gainesville shows how compliance with an equity-zone deployment requirement coexisted with unequal use when monitoring was not connected to binding review or corrective action. I did not estimate causal effects or claim that the proposed mechanisms are necessary or sufficient across all settings. This study’s research contribution is a theoretically grounded and empirically traceable institutional design that can be tested, refined, or rejected through comparative planning research.Takeaway for practice Planning agencies can adapt the framework through risk-tiered requirements: Routine applications might require brief records and manager-level review, whereas consequential or distributionally significant uses should receive more extensive scrutiny. For consequential uses, agencies should document the evidence supporting authorization, assign responsibility for equity review, publish accessible accountability information, specify thresholds for reconsideration, and require periodic evidence-based renewal. Procurement terms and vendor contracts can support these functions by preserving access, audit, change-control, and termination rights.

items.title: Accounting for large language masses: a time capsule
items.abstract: We present the time capsule of an e-mail conversation between the editors and co-editors of this journal that we have painstakingly reconstructed from the data-dust bowl of the late 2020s. Contributions to this conversation illustrate the struggles among journal editors who were dealing with the high number of journal submissions accompanying the arrival of generative AI around that time. They also highlight some of the human eccentricities in figuring out editorial and occupational strategies in a battle for intellectual hegemony, which people of that time will have thought they were losing. Whilst some of their despair is shrouded by the articulation of archaic concerns with efficiency or critical scholarship, the undeniable lostness of the human position we now experience will be particularly obvious to the reader in the more confident-sounding contributions to this historic debate.

items.title: Act4R: Action-conditioned 4D reconstruction for kinematics-free control
items.abstract: Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling. Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action. Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow. To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction. After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction. Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.

items.title: Adapting Collegiate Data Science Curricula for LLMs, Generative AI, and Beyond: Perspectives from Career Data Scientists
items.abstract: AI-based tools, generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) are transforming what it means to work and learn within the data science profession. We argue that higher education instructors should consider if, how, and in what ways to adapt data science curricula and pedagogy so that students who aspire to become data scientists are aware of how AI-based tools are integrated into and influencing the profession. To gain a sense of what modifications should be made to data science curricula (and why), we interviewed data science professionals across a variety of industry domains. We asked them to describe their career preparation, current work, and how employers expect them to use artificial intelligence tools and LLMs. Our findings suggest a general consensus that frequent human-AI interaction is necessary. A growing presence of AI tools in the workforce signals a stronger shift toward data pipelining, stakeholder communication and collaboration, and knowledge of evaluating AI output with epistemic expertise. Data professionals posed suggestions about how higher education might incorporate AI, generative AI, and LLMs into curricula, assessment, and practice, although some recommendations (e.g., learning to code with AI agents) would require a careful re-examination of the epistemic goals of data science by instructors. We illustrate how we took up professionals’ suggestions and adapted an undergraduate data science course designed for AI-integration in response. We conclude with a reflection on data science instructional challenges and potential roles that industry-academia collaborations might play in the AI era.

items.title: Addressing trust and distrust in artificial intelligence in newspaper texts
items.abstract: Abstract Trust in new technologies is often seen as a key condition for their implementation in everyday life, as the aim is for users to utilise technical innovations without strong reservations. The aspect of trust also plays a fundamental role in the discourse on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its far-reaching consequences for people’s lives. In this context, journalistic reporting as part of the public discourse plays a considerable role in creating trust or distrust in AI as a new technology. Whether and how trust issues are addressed in journalistic reporting has not been investigated so far. The paper explores how AI is depicted in German journalistic coverage, covering the topics of autonomous driving and smart home systems, which we expected to generate diverging trust issues. Furthermore, we show how trustworthiness and untrustworthiness are constructed in those texts, choosing AI applications intended for everyday use and therefore relying on trust from users ( Tschopp et al. 2022 ; Gillespie et al. 2021 ). We carried out a qualitative linguistic content analysis on a corpus of German press texts from 2023 that are dedicated to the aforementioned topics. We focused our analysis on explicit and implicit trust communication in the journalistic coverage of AI and examined whether qualitative differences can be identified in the way trust or distrust is addressed in various sub-discourses.

items.title: Advanced In Vitro Platforms for Experimental Liver Research: From Organoids and Liver‐on‐Chip to Omics and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Hepatocytes perform essential physiological functions in the human body. Gaining more profound insight into the liver structure, diseases, and physiology by using in vitro models can help to propose more relevant clinical applications. Conventional in vitro liver models, such as two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures, fail to adequately replicate the hepatic microenvironment, even when improved by adding additional cell types and extracellular matrix (ECM). These models do not address all necessary key components to mimic in vivo conditions, particularly multicellularity, specific ECM, and proper biophysical and biochemical parameters. Organoids, 3D-bioprinted constructs, and liver-on-chip platforms establish physiologically relevant models by improving cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions and multicellular architecture. For a comprehensive understanding of the liver's interconnections with related tissues and organs, a multi-organ-on-chip is a useful platform for more systemic studies. Also, other interdisciplinary approaches, particularly omics and artificial intelligence (AI), can enhance the accuracy of experimental and pre-clinical data achieved by such advanced in vitro liver platforms. This review highlights developing platforms for integrated approaches in experimental liver studies to enable researchers to have a holistic view of the liver in physiologic and pathologic conditions.

items.title: Advances in monitoring the injured brain
items.abstract: Multimodal neuromonitoring has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Traditional monitoring approaches based on intracranial pressure (ICP) and clinical examination alone have proven insufficient to capture the complex, heterogeneous pathophysiology that drives secondary brain injury. Over the past decade, significant advances in monitoring technology, including brain tissue oxygenation, cerebral microdialysis, continuous electroencephalography, near‑infrared spectroscopy, cerebrovascular autoregulation assessment and non‑invasive techniques have enabled clinicians to individualize treatment strategies based on real‑time physiological data. Concurrently, artificial intelligence and machine learning are transforming data integration and prognostic modelling, and non‑invasive and wearable approaches are beginning to extend brain monitoring beyond high‑resource neuro‑ICUs. This review examines recent innovations in neuromonitoring for TBI, highlighting invasive and non‑invasive modalities, their integration into multimodal platforms, and emerging technologies that promise to make precision neurocritical care a clinical reality. As we move toward the future of neurosurgery, the challenge lies not only in developing advanced monitoring tools but in interpreting them in the context of host‑specific factors and translating complex physiological signals into timely, evidence‑based interventions that improve patient outcomes.

items.title: Advances in Precision Agriculture Using AI
items.abstract: Precision agriculture (PA) is revolutionizing modern farming by integrating advanced digital technologies to optimize agricultural productivity, resource efficiency, and environmental sustainability. The infusion of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, has further transformed PA, enabling real-time decision-making, predictive analytics, and automation across the agricultural value chain. This chapter presents an in-depth overview of the core technologies that underpin AI-driven PA, including ML techniques, deep neural networks, Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, blockchain, and remote sensing. Further, this chapter explores how these technologies converge to support critical agricultural applications such as precision sowing, smart spraying, harvest optimization, pest and disease control, and crop health monitoring. Further, interoperability standards and the need for cohesive data frameworks are examined to ensure seamless integration of diverse PA tools. Challenges related to adoption, cost, data governance, algorithmic bias, and geospatial disparities are discussed, along with strategies for equitable technology deployment. The chapter also highlights participatory innovation models like Living Labs and User-Centered Design to promote inclusive development. Two case studies are also discussed that demonstrate practical AI applications in the field. Finally, the chapter underscores the transformative potential of AI in reshaping agriculture for a sustainable and food-secure future.

items.title: Adversary Simulation Design Frameworks for Proactive Cyber Defense in Complex Environments
items.abstract: The increasing sophistication and frequency of cyber threats in complex enterprise environments necessitates proactive approaches to cybersecurity. Adversary simulation, encompassing techniques such as red teaming, attack emulation, and threat scenario modeling, provides organizations with actionable insights into vulnerabilities, control effectiveness, and operational resilience. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for designing adversary simulations that are structured, repeatable, and aligned with organizational risk management objectives. The framework integrates threat intelligence, attack path modeling, system architecture analysis, and behavioral analytics to enable organizations to anticipate and mitigate potential cyberattacks before they occur. Key contributions include a systematic method for mapping threat vectors, designing attack scenarios, and prioritizing defensive investments based on quantified risk exposure. Scenario-based validation demonstrates that implementing the proposed framework enhances situational awareness, supports continuous improvement of defensive measures, and provides measurable benefits in risk reduction, resource allocation, and incident response readiness. The study concludes that organizations adopting structured adversary simulation frameworks can significantly improve proactive cyber defense capabilities, particularly in environments characterized by complex interdependencies, regulatory constraints, and rapidly evolving threat landscapes

items.title: Age- and sex-based clustering of foot dimensions in northwest Iran
items.abstract: Ethnicity and sex influence foot dimensions, essential for ergonomic footwear to reduce injury. This study analyzes Azeri men and women in Iran’s northwestern region; 4,297 subjects’ feet aged 20–60 were scanned; 3,122 healthy feet were selected. Twenty-nine foot anthropometric dimensions were computed via Python (2021). Principal component analysis (PCA) using SPSS (26) reduced these to three principal components (PCs) explaining most variance in foot shape. K-means clustering was applied across eight age subgroups (AG 1 –AG 8 ) and the total group (AG T ), with clustering quality assessed using the Davies–Bouldin index. Key findings revealed significant sex-related differences in foot dimensions ( p < 0.00). Regarding age-related differences, significant variations were observed in length, girth, and height dimensions for women (p-values: 0.00–0.03), while for men, only length showed significant age-related changes ( p = 0.00). In the total group, PC1–PC3 represented length, width/girth, and height in men, and girth, length, and height in women, respectively. Cluster analysis classified feet into small, medium, and large categories, with medium size being the most common across all age subgroups except AG3. Forefoot shape analysis revealed that men predominantly exhibited Egyptian, Semi-Roman, and Greek types, while women primarily showed Egyptian and Semi-Roman types, with the Egyptian type being the most frequent in both sexes. These findings support age- and sex-specific footwear design, especially for foot length in men and girth in women, and provide a quantitative basis for region-specific manufacturing, potentially improving foot health and offering economic benefits for local producers.

items.title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
items.abstract: Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. items.title: agent-risk: Risk Assessment for Changes to AI Agents
items.abstract: Before changing a deployed AI agent (a stricter safety gate, a new model), organizations must approve the change, starting from existing logs. Extending classical risk analysis to partial records and partial changes to running systems, agent-risk replays logged episodes, assuming nothing else changes and the agent does not anticipate the change. The log settles episodes acting as before, a declared stop value settles stopped ones, and the rest need logged support, a saved-state rerun, or a bound. We prove what logs must record for exact replay and which saved states serve a gate family. For independent episodes, we bound the reruns a decision needs and tolerable drift from live behavior. In a bash sandbox, a 7,200-episode log alone decided neither of two retry gates, which let the agent act after refusals the log never shows. Rerunning only each gate's blocked episodes from saved states reached both live decisions at half the agent calls of a live test sized post hoc for them, given the log. Without per-step harm, a stopping gate's certified harm ceiling rose up to 2.5-fold, since the log hides whether harm preceded the stop. Approval thus needs evidence designed in advance: log fields, saved states, targeted reruns.

items.title: Agentic AI-driven human digital twins for personalized healthcare: a comprehensive survey
items.abstract: Abstract Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are an innovative concept in the field of personalized medicine, relying on real-time models of a human body formed via collection and analysis of physiological, clinical, behavioural, and environmental data. Research on HDTs gives evidence to a considerable promise in terms of disease predictions, patient management, therapy optimization, and clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, existing technologies suffer from incomplete multimodal data integration, low-level of independent intelligence, missing reasoning possibilities, and non-adaptive decision making, which are vital for the development of sophisticated smart healthcare systems. Technological advancements are bringing in a new incorporating idea of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), which may help to solve the outlined limitations and to bring autonomous reasoning, multimodal learning, and intelligent support to clinical practice. This survey aims to review Agentic AI-led HDTs for personalized medicine, concentrating on the interrelation between HDTs and Multimodal Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Vision-Language Models, and autonomous artificial intelligence agents Our study discusses the history, models, supporting technologies, multiple data sources, and clinical uses of HDTs, along with the analysis of Agentic AI approaches that can be applied for flexible decision-making, continuous patient monitoring, and individualized treatment development. Besides, this survey consists of comparative analysis of existing research works where methods, advantages, disadvantages, and research challenges are specified. There are also serious issues discussed, like interoperability, justification, confidentiality ensuring, safety, ethical regulation, clinical testing and legal compliance, etc. And finally, we specify prospects of research within the fields of self-adaptive digital twins, reliable autonomous health agents, federated intelligence, edge AI and multimodal foundations focused on healthcare.

items.title: AI Adoption and Trading Performance Analysis: Study on Retail Futures and Options Traders of Karnataka
items.abstract: Retail participation in India’s Futures and Options (F&O) market has grown rapidly, and AI-based trading tools are now widely available to individual traders, yet regulatory data indicate that most individual derivative traders incur net losses. Existing studies have largely examined why investors adopt AI tools and not whether adoption improves trading outcomes. This study examines the correlation between AI adoption and trading performance among retail F&O traders in six cities of Karnataka, with Trading Decision Quality as the mediating mechanism and Financial Literacy as the moderating condition. Data was gathered using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire from 401 retail Foreign Exchange (F&O) traders and evaluate using Exploratory Factor Analysis (SPSS) and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (SmartPLS, 5,000 bootstrap resamples). AI Adoption was identified as a construct consisting of three factors, namely, Perceived Usefulness and Continued Reliance, Perceived Ease of Use, and Trust in AI Reliability. It can be seen that AI Adoption has a positive impact on both Trading Decision Quality and Trading Performance. Trading Decision Quality acts as a partial mediator in the correlation between AI Adoption and Trading Performance, which means that the use of AI tools leads to favourable results by virtue of facilitating higher quality decisions while trading. Financial Literacy plays a positive moderating role in the influence of AI Adoption on Trading Performance, implying that traders with higher levels of financial literacy reap more advantages from AI tools. items.title: AI Cloud Platform for Smart City Traffic Monitoring and Analysis Using Multi-Dimensional Big Data and Deep Learning Models
items.abstract: Rapid urbanization and persistent road-safety challenges have increased the demand for intelligent traffic management systems capable of supporting traffic monitoring, incident analysis, and short-term forecasting. Existing artificial intelligence solutions frequently address these functions through separate, task-specific applications, making it difficult for traffic operators to access heterogeneous analytical services within a common operational environment. This study presents a cloud-based, multi-source traffic intelligence platform that incorporates independent analytical services for CCTV video, UAV video, and IoT sensor data. The proposed platform performs platform-level service integration among the three sources. Its principal analytical component is a multi-model, multi-task UAV video framework consisting of three task-specific pipelines for accident detection and classification, emergency-vehicle detection, and vehicle tracking, counting, and congestion analysis. The semantic outputs of these pipelines are integrated at the decision level to generate annotated videos, traffic statistics, congestion assessments, incident alerts, and consolidated traffic reports. YOLOv8-based models are used for traffic-object and incident detection, Deep SORT is employed for multi-object tracking, and DCRNN is independently applied to PeMS-BAY sensor data for short-term traffic forecasting. A graph-partitioning strategy with overlapping boundary nodes is also evaluated to investigate the trade-off between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency. Module-level experiments demonstrate effective task-specific performance. The CCTV accident detection model achieves a validation precision of 89.09%, recall of 88.10%, and mAP of 88.09%. The augmented UAV accident-analysis model achieves a validation precision of 82.20% and mAP of 80.20%. For five-minute traffic forecasting, the DCRNN service obtains an MAE of 0.85, MAPE of 1.63%, and RMSE of 1.54 on the PeMS-BAY dataset. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating independently processed traffic-analysis services within a common cloud platform while using multi-model UAV analytics to provide consolidated aerial traffic intelligence.

items.title: AI conversational agents as population health infrastructure: promise, peril, and the case for public-interest design
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from novelty to infrastructure. Rulebased chatbots that once nudged users through smoking-cessation scripts have given way to large language model (LLM)-powered agents capable of open-ended, multilingual, empathetic-sounding dialogue, available around the clock at near-zero marginal cost. Systematic and scoping reviews now document measurable effects of AI chatbots on physical activity, diet, smoking cessation, medication adherence, and mental distress across thousands of participants (Feng et al., 2025). The World Health Organization (WHO) itself has deployed a generative AI assistant, S.A.R.A.H., to test population-scale health communication (van Kolfschooten et al., 2025). Taken together, these developments justify treating conversational AI not merely as a clinical or commercial curiosity, but as an emerging layer of public health infrastructure -one that sits alongside water systems, mass media, and vaccination programs as a determinant of how populations receive, interpret, and act on health information. (Wang et al., 2024). This opinion argues that the digital public health community should engage conversational AI on exactly those terms: as infrastructure, not gadgetry. Infrastructure framing changes the questions we ask. Instead of "does the chatbot work?" we should ask who it works for, under what governance, and with what consequences for equity, trust, and the broader information ecosystem. I organize this argument around three tensions that recur across the recent literature: (i) genuine behavioral efficacy versus fragile evidentiary depth; (ii) the promise of expanded access versus the risk of a new digital divide; and (iii) the communicative power of generative AI versus its capacity to manufacture and amplify misinformation. I close by proposing that Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)aligned public health institutions adopt a public-interest design standard for conversational AI, rather than leaving its trajectory to consumer technology markets alone.The evidence base for AI chatbots in health promotion has grown quickly and, on balance, positively. A widely cited systematic review found that AI chatbots produced favorable outcomes across lifestyle modification domains, particularly physical activity, diet, and smoking cessation (Aggarwal et al., 2023). A 2026 scoping review of 43 studies (Fu et al., 2026) reported that 82% of behavior-change comparisons trended positive, though only about a third reached moderate or larger effect sizes, and cost-effectiveness data were essentially absent. A meta-analysis focused on adolescents and young adults (Feng et al., 2025) similarly found chatbots effective for alleviating mental distress and supporting health behaviors, while noting substantial heterogeneity in intervention design and outcome measurement. Three limitations temper enthusiasm. First, most trials are short, nonclinical, adult-skewed, and rarely randomized at scale; only about a third of studies in the largest recent scoping review were randomized controlled trials (Fu et al., 2026). Second, "AI chatbot" spans an enormous range of systems, from rule-based decision trees to frontier LLMs, and pooling them obscures which architectural features actually drive behavior change (Kurniawan et al., 2024;Schachner et al., 2020). Third, almost no study reports durability beyond a few months, leaving open whether early engagement gains represent sustained health improvement or a novelty effect. For a section whose remit is population-level promotion and prevention rather than individual clinical outcomes, this matters: infrastructure decisions built on inflated short-term efficacy claims risk premature, poorly targeted public investment (Hampsher-Monk et al., 2024).A second tension concerns reach. Proponents rightly note that AI chatbots are inexpensive to scale, available in multiple languages, and can operate where clinical workforce is scarceattributes explicitly cited in WHO's own rationale for deploying S.A.R.A.H. as a research prototype for population health communication (Palmer & Schwan, 2025). Behavioralaccess frameworks extend this logic, arguing that digital health tools must be evaluated not only on availability but on whether populations can meaningfully engage with them across design, delivery, dissemination, and sustainment stages. Yet the same structural gaps that limit telemedicine and mobile health also constrain chatbot benefit: broadband access, device ownership, digital literacy, language coverage, and trust in institutional actors are unevenly distributed within and between countries (Banerjee, 2026). Chatbots trained and validated predominantly in high-resource, English-language settings may perform less reliably for populations with the greatest unmet need -the same populations digital public health is meant to prioritize under SDG 3, 9, and 11's emphasis on inclusive infrastructure and sustainable, resilient communities. A chatbot that reduces cost-per-contact for a health system does not automatically reduce disparities in outcomes; without equity-explicit design, deployment, and evaluation, it may simply reallocate existing advantages to those already best served by digital tools, echoing patterns already observed in AI-enabled primary care and telemedicine expansion (Elangovan et al., 2025).The third tension is the sharpest. The same generative capacity that lets an AI chatbot deliver personalized, conversational health guidance also lets it generate fluent, plausible-sounding health misinformation, and do so faster than human fact-checkers can respond. A 2025 opinion piece in this journal warned that generative AI tools function as de facto triage systems and informal health advisors in low-and middle-income countries, where their fluency can be mistaken for authority even when their outputs are unreliable. A parallel systematic review of generative AI and health misinformation catalogued mechanisms of production, propagation, and mitigation across text, image, and synthetic media, underscoring that the problem is not hypothetical but already observed at scale (Saeidnia et al., 2026). Mitigation research is advancing in step. Retrieval-augmented generation has been used to improve the factual reliability of LLM-based COVID-19 fact-checking tools (Li et al., 2025), and thematic-analysis pipelines have been proposed to detect and "inoculate" audiences against circulating misinformation narratives (Malek et al., 2026). A recent risk taxonomy specifically for public health LLM adoption (Zhou et al., 2025) offers a structured way for practitioners to reason about failure modes before deployment rather than after. Conversational AI for vaccine communication, an earlier and instructive precedent, showed both promise for addressing hesitancy and clear risk of amplifying inaccurate claims when systems were insufficiently curated (Passanante et al., 2023). The lesson across this literature is consistent: the communicative power of conversational AI is not neutral infrastructure like a water pipe; it actively shapes the epistemic environment it operates in, for better or worse, depending on design choices made well upstream of any individual conversation.Evidence highlights Population-level implication Efficacy vs. evidentiary depth ~82% of behavior-change comparisons favorable, but only ~1/3 with moderate+ effect sizes; RCTs a minority (Fu et al., 2026) provenance, and risk taxonomies (Zhou et al., 2025) prior to releaseNone of this argues against conversational AI in public health; the direction of the evidence is cautiously positive, and the WHO's own experimentation with S.A.R.A.H. reflects institutional recognition that this technology will be used regardless of academic ambivalence. The argument is instead for treating conversational AI the way public health has learned, sometimes painfully, to treat other infrastructure: as a shared resource whose design choices carry population-level consequences, and which therefore warrants governance commensurate with its reach. Three concrete commitments follow. First, funders and health systems evaluating AI chatbot interventions should require reporting of architecture (rulebased versus LLM-based, retrieval-augmented or not), population stratification by digitalaccess indicators, and effect durability beyond the intervention period -the absence of which currently limits comparability across the field (Fu et al., 2026). Second, deployment in low-resource or multilingual settings should be preceded by equity-focused validation rather than assumed from high-resource pilot data, consistent with behavioral-access frameworks that treat dissemination and sustainment as distinct design stages, not afterthoughts. Third, any public health-facing conversational agent should be built on retrieval-grounded, provenance-transparent architectures and evaluated against a structured risk taxonomy before release, rather than relying on post hoc misinformation cleanup. WHO's 2024 guidance on large multimodal models already articulates comparable principles -transparency, accountability, and human oversight -for governments and developers; the task now is operationalizing them at the level of individual chatbot deployments rather than treating them as abstract commitments.The digital public health field has an opportunity, still open but narrowing, to shape how conversational AI is integrated into population health promotion before deployment patterns harden into path dependency. The evidence reviewed here suggests genuine, if still shallow, behavioral benefit; genuine, if unevenly distributed, gains in access; and genuine, dual-use communicative power that can either strengthen or corrode public trust in health information depending on how it is engineered and governed. Framing conversational AI as infrastructure rather than as a discrete clinical tool has practical consequences: it shifts evaluation from short efficacy trials toward equity-stratified, durability-tested, misinformation-resilient deployment standards, and it shifts responsibility from individual developers toward the institutions, including public health agencies, research funders, and journals such as this one, that decide what counts as sufficient evidence for scale. A reasonable objection is that infrastructure-level governance risks slowing beneficial innovation, particularly in settings where any accessible health guidance outperforms none. That concern is legitimate and argues for proportionate, tiered oversight rather than uniform restriction -lighter validation for low-stakes wellness nudges, more rigorous requirements for agents addressing vaccine hesitancy, chronic disease self-management, or crisis-adjacent mental health support. What the evidence does not support is treating conversational AI's current trajectory as selfcorrecting. Left to consumer technology incentives alone, generative health chatbots are likely to continue optimizing for engagement and fluency rather than for population-level epidemiological benefit or equitable reach. The digital public health community is well positioned, through funding priorities, publication standards, and partnership with bodies like WHO, to redirect that trajectory toward public-interest design before it further consolidates around existing digital and geographic advantage.

items.title: AI Ensemble Framework for OSINT-Based Social Media Crime Prevention in Kenya
items.abstract: Criminal networks increasingly exploit social media to organize, recruit, incite, and coordinate unlawful activities, whereas law-enforcement monitoring in Kenya remains largely manual and English-centric. This study aimed to design, implement, and rigorously evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) ensemble framework for open-source intelligence (OSINT) classification of crime- and threat-relevant content in Kenya's trilingual (English, Kiswahili, and Sheng) and code-switched digital environment. A corpus of 6,212 documents was assembled from six sources: Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and two Sheng-language corpora. The corpus was weakly labelled using a 214-term trilingual crime-and-threat lexicon. Label noise was quantified against a manually annotated stratified validation sample (n = 320), yielding Cohen's κ = 0.350, silver-label precision of 0.525, and recall of 0.750. Combined word- and character-level term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features comprising 25,831 dimensions were used to train a hyperparameter-tuned, weighted soft-voting ensemble consisting of multinomial naive Bayes, a calibrated linear support vector machine, random forest, logistic regression, and XGBoost. The decision threshold was calibrated using cross-validated out-of-fold probabilities. The optimized ensemble achieved 98.3% accuracy, 80.6% precision, 62.5% recall, 70.4% F1-score, 0.907 ROC-AUC, 0.724 PR-AUC, 0.702 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and a 0.50% false-positive rate. The ensemble outperformed the best single learner and a frozen multilingual transformer baseline (F1 = 26.2%). Ablation analysis demonstrated the contribution of the Sheng-normalization layer, while comparison of class-imbalance strategies showed that cost-sensitive learning combined with threshold calibration produced the strongest overall performance compared with SMOTE-based resampling. The findings demonstrate that linguistically inclusive classical machine-learning ensembles can provide an accurate, auditable, and computationally deployable approach to proactive social-media crime prevention in low-resource, code-switched settings. The study also derives policy implications concerning threshold-calibrated triage, expert annotation, data-protection impact assessments, and safeguards against dual-use misuse.

items.title: AI Fitness OS: Verifiable, Multi-Metric Fitness Guidance by Constraining a Large Language Model with Deterministically Computed Targets
items.abstract: Fitness applications usually record one behaviour in isolation, and large-language-model (LLM) coaches produce fluent advice whose numbers are rarely checked. This paper presents AI Fitness OS, a web application that keeps training, nutrition, hydration, sleep, weight, steps and goals in one per-user record, computes every numerical target deterministically from published equations and stated heuristics, and passes those targets to Google Gemini as binding constraints; each generated meal plan is re-checked in code against a ±5 % tolerance. The premise was examined through secondary research on a public dataset of 2,111 records, and the artefact through tests, simulation and live measurement. All eight lifestyle metrics that the system tracks or addresses were significantly associated with obesity level (Bonferroni-adjusted α = 0.00625), although only three remained so on 515 records resembling the original survey. A Random Forest that combined the eight metrics reached a macro-F1 of 0.720 against 0.263 for the best single metric (Wilcoxon W = 55, p = 0.00098). Across 1,000 simulated user profiles, every constrained meal plan fell within ±5 % of its calorie target, against 75 of 1,000 unconstrained plans (exact McNemar p < 10⁻²⁰⁰). The calculator agreed with the dataset's weight-category labels for 98.82 % of records, and live responses took 2.5–6.1 s at no cost. The findings support computing arithmetic, generating language and checking the output against the computed numbers.

items.title: AI for Solar Energy Systems
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of solar energy has accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve forecasting accuracy, photovoltaic performance, intelligent control, fault diagnosis, energy storage management, and smart grid operation. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning, Digital Twins, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Edge AI, Federated Learning, and Generative AI have transformed solar energy systems into more adaptive and data-driven infrastructures. Despite these advances, challenges related to data quality, model generalization, computational efficiency, cybersecurity, and explainability continue to limit large-scale deployment. An integrated perspective is presented by connecting AI applications across photovoltaic systems, solar thermal technologies, energy storage, and intelligent energy networks within a unified renewable energy ecosystem. Emerging research trends and future directions highlight the evolution toward AI-native energy systems that support efficient, resilient, and sustainable intelligent societies.

items.title: AI for Wind Energy Systems
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the wind energy sector, marking a major step toward sustainable and intelligent societies. As global energy demands rise and carbon reduction becomes urgent, AI offers powerful tools to enhance the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of wind power systems. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and predictive analytics, AI optimizes turbine design, predictive maintenance, load forecasting, and smart grid integration. By leveraging big data from sensors, meteorological sources, and operational parameters, AI enables accurate wind prediction, timely fault detection, and real-time performance optimization. Additionally, AI-driven systems play an emerging role in urban wind integration by improving micro-wind utilization, energy storage, and distributed generation within smart cities. The chapter also addresses economic feasibility, environmental sustainability, and ethical implications of AI-enabled wind energy applications.

items.title: AI in Chemistry Education: A Thematic Narrative Review of Opportunities, Limitations, and Equity Gaps (2020–2026)
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted rapidly growing body of scholarship on the role in chemistry education since the public release of ChatGPT in the late of 2022. This thematic narrative review synthesizes 40 English-language sources including empirical studies, curriculum reports, and stakeholder surveys, and systematic/bibliometric reviews published between 2020 and 2026, identified through a structured, author-curated search of recent chemistry-education and analytical-chemistry literature (see Methodology). Sources were coded inductively and organized into six recurring themes: AI/ML literacy as curriculum content; AI-driven tutoring, personalization, and accessibility; empirical evaluations of generative AI's chemical reasoning; stakeholder perceptions; AI's transformation of chemistry research and scientific communication; and equity, ethics, and systemic barriers. Across the reviewed literature, a recurring position though not a formal consensus is that AI should support rather than replace human instruction. Empirical evaluations consistently report that large language models generate fluent but sometimes hallucinated or subtly incorrect chemistry content, particularly for visual and multi-representational reasoning tasks. The corpus is concentrated in higher education and high-income countries, and this pattern should be interpreted as a prominent tendency in the reviewed literature rather than a field-wide finding. Priorities for chemistry educators include critical AI literacy instruction, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and explicit attention to equity.

items.title: AI-Assisted Business Ideation as a Technology–Cognition–Institutional Pathway to Entrepreneurial Intention: A Serial Mediation Model of Perceived Feasibility and Entrepreneurial Consultancy Services
items.abstract: Generative AI has significantly reduced the effort and expense of developing and refining venture ideas, without eliminating the uncertainty and resource limitations of executing a venture. This research examines the potential of AI-assisted business ideation (AIBI) to drive behavioral change in accessing entrepreneurial support infrastructure. The study uses technology-cognition-institutional framework to examine the relationship between AIBI and perceived feasibility (PF) and entrepreneurial consultancy services engagement (ECS) and how these two variables mediate the relationship between AIBI and entrepreneurial intentions (EI). The study analyzed data from 319 university students in Pakistan using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). It evaluated the reliability and validity of the measurement model and examined structural relationships through bootstrapping with bias-corrected confidence intervals. Findings indicate that AI-based business ideation positively affects perceived feasibility, which in turn enhances engagement with entrepreneurial creative strategies (ECS).Moreover, ECS positively and significantly affect entrepreneurial intention, this in turn has a positive and significant direct effect on AIBI. The pathway from AIBI to perceived feasibility to engagement in entrepreneurial consultancy services to entrepreneurial intention is significant, emphasizing that AIBI affects entrepreneurial intention both cognitively and institutionally. This study extends AI entrepreneurship research by showing that AI's effects on entrepreneurial intention go beyond boosting entrepreneurial cognition. This study also contributes to existing intention models by conceptualizing entrepreneurial consultancy services as an endogenous behavioral mediator rather than a contextual condition, offering a more complete explanation of AI-enabled ideation's role in entrepreneurial readiness.

items.title: AI-Based Network Intrusion Detection System Using Machine Learning and Explainable AI
items.abstract: Network intrusion detection is an important cybersecurity function because network traffic can contain benign activity as well as malicious behavior. This paper presents an AI-based Network Intrusion Detection System (AI-NIDS) that combines live packet capture, flow generation, machine-learning classification, explainable artificial intelligence, and web-based visualization. The prototype is implemented in an Ubuntu virtual machine hosted through VirtualBox. Scapy captures traffic visible on the virtual network interface, and related packets are grouped into flows. Four features that can be derived directly from live traffic—destination port, packet count, total bytes, and average packet size—are used by the live classification pipeline. CICIDS2017 is used for model training and evaluation. Isolation Forest is used for anomaly-oriented analysis, while Random Forest and XGBoost perform multi-class classification. SHAP provides feature-level explanations, and a Flask dashboard presents live flows, detections, and explanations. On a held-out test set of 22,339 samples, Random Forest achieved 90.67% accuracy and XGBoost achieved 94.42% accuracy; macro F1 scores were 0.78 and 0.81, respectively. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining machine learning and explainability in a practical NIDS prototype, while highlighting limitations related to reduced live features, rare attack classes, false positives, and virtualized network scope.

items.title: AI-Driven Credit Scoring and Financial Justice among Young Entrepreneurs in Dhaka City: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: The lack of access to finance is a major issue for young entrepreneurs, especially those who have poor credit scores, lack financial statements and have no collateral. Artificial intelligence (AI) based credit scoring systems have been seen as a potential solution to credit assessment using alternative data, but there are concerns about fairness, transparency, accountability and algorithmic exclusion. This study aims to understand the impact of AI-powered credit scoring on financial justice for young entrepreneurs in Dhaka City, focusing on perceptions of financial access, AI-driven lending opportunities, ethical concerns, and responsible decision-making practices. The study uses a qualitative research approach and thematic analysis to explore the experiences and perspectives of entrepreneurs on traditional credit assessment systems and AI-powered lending mechanisms. The results show that AI-powered credit scoring is seen as a potential means to financial inclusion, as it can include alternative data like digital transaction records and business activity data. But there are also important issues of algorithmic bias, data quality, privacy, transparency, and the risk of leaving out people with small digital footprints, participants note. The study also shows that in the context of AI-driven lending, financial justice encompasses not merely the opportunity to obtain a loan, but also procedural fairness, transparency or explain ability, accountability, and the ability to object to or challenge automated decisions. The study adds to the literature on responsible AI and financial inclusion by offering a socio-technical approach that combines technological innovation and human-centered governance. The results indicate that AI-based credit scoring can contribute to inclusive entrepreneurial finance if applied in an ethically guided, transparent, and accountable manner with proper human supervision.

items.title: AI-Driven Governance in India: Balancing Administrative Efficiency, Transparency, Accountability and Data Protection
items.abstract: India is embedding artificial intelligence (AI) in public administration at the very moment its legal architecture for data protection, transparency and AI oversight is being rewritten. Between November 2025 and August 2026, the government issued the India AI Governance Guidelines, notified the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules 2025, hosted the AI Impact Summit, and began defending in the Supreme Court a constitutional challenge to the DPDP Act's amendment of the Right to Information (RTI) Act. This paper asks whether administrative efficiency, transparency, accountability and data protection can be reconciled in AI-driven governance in India. Using doctrinal analysis, policy analysis and a case study of Telangana's Samagra Vedika welfare-profiling system, it argues that the four values are not inherently opposed. The tensions arise from design choices, thin institutional capacity and broad exemptions for the State. The paper identifies four structural gaps: voluntary AI guidance without enforceable duties; consent-free State processing and wide exemptions under the DPDP Act; the narrowing of the RTI public-interest test; and the absence of a right to human review and explanation. It proposes a proportionality-based, risk-tiered framework combining statutory authorisation, impact assessments, algorithm registers, meaningful human review, independent audit and accessible redress. Legal positions are stated as at 28 September 2026.

items.title: AI-Driven One Health Surveillance for Zoonotic Risk Mitigation: Insights from TBE and CCHF
items.abstract: Emerging zoonoses, particularly vector-borne ones, are driven by climate change, biodiversity loss and land-use change. Surveillance, however, remains fragmented and largely reactive, and often fails to detect the risk signals that precede spillover. This narrative review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), integrated with georeferenced and climatic data, could support a transition toward predictive, anticipatory One Health surveillance. Using tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (CCHF) as case studies, we distinguish evidence from conventional statistical models, ML models and deep-learning applica-tions. ML models combining climatic, land-cover and host variables have shown promising ret-rospective performance in mapping tick habitat suitability and TBE and CCHF risk, whereas deep learning has been applied mainly to tick identification. However, AI evidence specific to TBE and CCHF remains limited: few disease-specific studies exist, validation is largely internal, no model has been evaluated prospectively, and some reported figures derive from synthetic data. We consider this gap a key finding. We also discuss data quality, model transferability, validation practices, al-gorithmic transparency and the EU AI Act. AI may enable a shift from costly emergency response toward validated Early Warning Systems if methodological, infrastructural and regulatory gaps are addressed. We outline priorities for researchers, veterinarians, clinicians and policymakers.

items.title: AI-Enabled Autonomous Area-Keeping for Underwater Vehicles
items.abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), commonly known as submarine drones, provide a critical capability for modern naval operations requiring persistent presence in contested and GPS denied environments. This paper addresses autonomous positioning and area keeping of AUVs within predefined underwater zones using integrated inertial, acoustic, and velocity based navigation systems. Artificial intelligence techniques, including machine learning–based sensor fusion and adaptive decision making, enhance state estimation, navigation robustness, and control performance in uncertain and dynamic environments. By combining AI enabled perception with robust control algorithms, AUVs can maintain precise station keeping and boundary awareness while compensating for ocean currents and environmental disturbances. These capabilities support force protection, intelligence gathering, and undersea surveillance missions, enabling discreet and sustained operations with minimal human intervention.
